prompt: A fintech company has an Amazon S3 bucket in Account A (the data account) that contains about 300 million settlement report objects. All objects are encrypted with SSE-KMS by using a customer managed AWS KMS key in Account A. A Lambda function in partner settlement Account B, which belongs to a separate organization, must read reports from this bucket every day before dawn. The company recently updated the bucket policy to allow s3:GetObject for the Account B execution role. However, the Lambda invocation fails with AccessDenied because of a KMS permissions error. The two accounts are not in the same AWS Organizations organization, so the issue cannot be resolved with organization-level policies. The data team (3 people) does not have the capacity for a large-scale effort to re-encrypt existing objects or rotate the key. During an external audit, the company must prove that this one role in Account B is the only external principal that can use the key, and the work must be completed this week. The partner manages the Account B Lambda code, so the code cannot be modified. The security team in Account A tracks key policy changes with AWS CloudTrail and reviews access permissions every quarter. The work must be finished before the next settlement deadline, and the only contact on the Account B side is one person on the partner's operations team. Which solution resolves the issue in the SAFEST way while maintaining the principle of least privilege?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Broaden the bucket policy to allow s3:* and change the Principal to the Account B root user so that the encryption error is bypassed.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Re-encrypt the objects with the AWS managed key (aws/s3) and add Account B to that key's policy so that both accounts share the same key.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Change the Principal in the key policy to * so that every AWS account can call kms:Decrypt, with no additional conditions or restrictions.

choices.label: D
choices.text: In the Account A key policy, allow kms:Decrypt for the specified role in Account B. Also allow kms:Decrypt on that key ARN in the IAM policy of the Account B role.

explanation: Allowing the action in both the key policy and the IAM policy is the correct answer. Cross-account use of a KMS key works only when the key policy in the account that owns the key allows the external account or role and the IAM policy in the external account delegates that permission. Either one alone is not enough. Broadening the bucket policy does not resolve the KMS permissions error and only makes the permissions excessive. An AWS managed key has a key policy that cannot be modified, so it cannot be shared with another account. Setting the key policy Principal to * opens decryption permission to every account, which directly violates the principle of least privilege. The constraint that re-encrypting 300 million objects is impractical supports the correct approach, which keeps the existing key, and counts against the option that requires re-encryption. The condition that the partner's code cannot be modified and the audit condition that key usage must be narrowed to a single role are satisfied by only the correct answer.

prompt: The platform team at a healthcare information company uses AWS CloudFormation to deploy the same Amazon S3 bucket stack template to 12 accounts. The template does not define the BucketEncryption property at all and leaves default encryption to the service default. One day, an operator used the console to change the default encryption of one bucket to a different KMS key, but the stack drift detection that runs every morning on an Amazon EventBridge schedule reported IN_SYNC. This stack is part of a regulated system, so any arbitrary change in the console that differs from the stack definition becomes an audit finding. The security team wants manual changes like this to be detected as drift too, and wants to keep the stack structure and deployment pipeline as unchanged as possible and minimize changes. There is no dedicated automation staff, and the current detection schedule and notification setup already work correctly. The stack is deployed on its own with no parent stack, the bucket policy and lifecycle rules are defined in the same template, and template changes can follow the existing process that includes code review. The security team receives the drift results in a report every morning and does not want to change this reporting cadence. Which action is MOST appropriate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Change the scheduled job so that drift detection runs at the nested stack level instead of on the parent stack, so that the bucket resource in the nested stack is also included in the scan.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Remove the bucket from the stack and then import it again with an import operation. The entire actual configuration is then stored as the baseline, and changes to any property are detected as drift afterward.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Explicitly define BucketEncryption with the desired value in the template, update the stack, and then run drift detection. The property is tracked only if it is stated explicitly, even when the value is the same as the default.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Instead of drift detection, create a recurring deployment schedule that runs a stack update with the same template every day so that manually changed properties are overwritten based on the template.

explanation: The correct answer is to explicitly define the BucketEncryption property in the template. CloudFormation evaluates drift only for property values that are explicitly specified in the template or parameters, and it does not track properties that are not defined or that rely on defaults. Therefore the property must be stated explicitly, even when the value is the same as the default, for a manual change to be reported as drift. Running detection at the nested stack level only compensates for the fact that a parent stack does not scan its nested stacks. This bucket is not in a nested stack, so that is unrelated to the cause. Importing is also based on the properties defined in the template, so properties that are not defined still go untracked. Redeploying the same template does not change properties that are not in the template, so the manual change is not overwritten. The background that the detection schedule and notifications already work confirms that the cause is not the detection method but the missing property in the template. Because the stack is not nested, the option that changes the detection unit is unrelated to the cause.

prompt: An online restaurant reservation service runs on an Amazon ECS service across two Availability Zones behind an Application Load Balancer. From midnight to 6 AM there is almost no traffic, so alarms based on ALB request metrics often go into INSUFFICIENT_DATA. Recently, after a front-end deployment, an incident occurred in which the seat selection screen returned a blank page with HTTP 200, and the company learned about it only after customer inquiries came in. The three-step screen flow of login, seat selection, and payment confirmation is linked by a session cookie issued after login, and the check must also confirm that a reservation number is displayed on the last screen. When the flow breaks, it must be detected at 1-minute intervals before customers notice, and an alert must reach the on-call engineer within 3 minutes of the failure. The check script must run from outside without modifying production code. A separate test account is used for the checks, so no real payments occur, and notifications are already connected through Amazon SNS to the on-call engineer's paging app. The operations team has 3 people, and a development slot to update the check script is scheduled once per quarter. Which solution BEST meets these requirements without depending on user traffic?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Lower the threshold of the ALB HTTPCode_Target_5XX_Count alarm to 1 and configure the alarm to treat missing data as breaching.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Run a CloudWatch Synthetics canary that executes the three-step browser workflow at 1-minute intervals, and create an alarm on the SuccessPercent metric.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Use a Route 53 health check with string matching on the payment confirmation URL's response, and receive the health check failure alarm through Amazon SNS.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Create a metric filter for ERROR in the application logs, set an alarm to trigger when the 5-minute sum is 1 or greater, and increase log retention.

explanation: A Synthetics canary is the correct answer. A canary runs a script on a schedule along the same path as a real customer, supports an interval as short as 1 minute, and emits result metrics even when there is no traffic, so it detects a break at any step of the flow first. A 5xx metric alarm cannot catch cases where the flow breaks with a 200 response, and treating missing data as breaching causes repeated false positives during low-traffic hours. A Route 53 health check is a single-request check, so it cannot verify a multi-step flow from login to payment confirmation. A log-based filter produces no logs when there is no traffic, so there is no detection signal at all. The conditions that the incident was a screen that broke with a 200 response and that the flow has three steps linked by a session cookie eliminate the single-URL check and the options based on error metrics. The condition of a multi-step flow linked by a session cookie eliminates the single-URL check and the error-metric-based alarm.

prompt: The infrastructure team at a SaaS company deploys the same AWS CloudFormation template to three environments: development, staging, and production. The AWS::EC2::Volume resource in the template is the data volume, and the operations team plans an update that changes the AvailabilityZone property to move the volume to a different Availability Zone. Changing this property causes the resource to be replaced. This change was initiated because last quarter, data was lost by mistake during a stack update and deletion. The data on the replaced old volume must be recoverable even after the update succeeds, and the volume data must also remain when the stack is deleted later. Keeping the old volume as is not an acceptable cost, and only snapshot storage costs are acceptable. The solution must be achieved with the template alone, without manual procedures by operators. The template also defines an EC2 instance and a security group in addition to the data volume. The audit team verifies that the old data can be restored within 30 days after the replacement, and the operations team already has a process of previewing the impact with change sets. The stack is in the Seoul Region, the volume size is 500 GiB, and the change is scheduled for the early-morning maintenance window next Tuesday. Which template change is MOST appropriate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Have an operator manually create a volume snapshot immediately before the update, leave the template unchanged, and run the update. Create a manual snapshot in the same way before deleting the stack.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Specify both UpdateReplacePolicy: Snapshot and DeletionPolicy: Snapshot on the volume resource.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Specify DeletionPolicy: Retain and UpdateReplacePolicy: Retain on the volume resource so that the old volume remains intact after it is replaced or deleted.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Specify only DeletionPolicy: Snapshot on the volume resource so that the deletion policy is applied when a replacement occurs and a snapshot of the old volume is created.

explanation: The correct answer is to specify both UpdateReplacePolicy and DeletionPolicy as Snapshot. UpdateReplacePolicy determines what happens to the old resource when a property change causes it to be replaced, while DeletionPolicy applies only when the stack or the resource definition is deleted and does not apply to replacement. EC2 volumes support snapshots, so specifying Snapshot for both leaves only a snapshot in both replacement and deletion. Specifying only the deletion policy causes the old volume to be deleted by default during replacement, which violates the requirement. Retain keeps the entire old volume, which continues to be billed and violates the cost constraint that only snapshots are allowed. A manual snapshot violates the constraint that the solution must be achieved with the template alone. The cost constraint that allows only snapshot storage eliminates Retain, and the constraint that the solution must use the template alone eliminates the manual snapshot.

prompt: The real-time battle servers of a mobile game company communicate over UDP and run as Amazon ECS Fargate services behind Network Load Balancers in the Seoul and Tokyo Regions. Peak concurrent users are about 200,000. Some older clients hardcode the server IP in the app or cache DNS responses for a long time, so with Route 53 failover, switching during a Regional failure is delayed by several minutes or more. The solution must keep static IP addresses without changing the clients and must automatically switch to the other Region when one Region has no healthy endpoints. Connection latency to the battle servers is important, so users must be connected to the nearest healthy Region, and app store update review takes 2 weeks, so changing the clients is difficult. The operations staff is also small, and the company does not want to operate its own fleet of proxy servers. The game servers communicate on UDP port 7777, normally 70% of connections go to Seoul and 30% to Tokyo, and the development team has no capacity to change server and client code in this quarter's season update. The backend in both Seoul and Tokyo consists of 40 ECS Fargate tasks, and the configuration in the two Regions is identical. Which solution BEST meets these requirements?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Assign an Elastic IP address to the Seoul NLB and have clients use this IP address. If a failure occurs, an operator runs a script to reassociate the Elastic IP address with the NLB in the Tokyo Region.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Create an AWS Global Accelerator standard accelerator, register the NLBs in both Regions as endpoint groups, and have clients use the accelerator's static anycast IP addresses.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Create an Amazon CloudFront distribution, configure the NLBs in both Regions as an origin group, and set up origin failover so that requests are passed to the secondary origin if the primary origin fails.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Lower the TTL of the Route 53 failover records to 5 seconds and attach health checks to the NLBs in both Regions so that Route 53 responds with the Tokyo NLB if the Seoul health check fails.

explanation: The correct answer is a Global Accelerator standard accelerator. An accelerator provides static anycast IP addresses and automatically routes traffic to healthy endpoints based on endpoint health. It does not depend on DNS caching, so there is no issue with clients that ignore TTL, and it supports both TCP and UDP. Lowering the Route 53 TTL does not solve the problems of clients that do not honor TTL and hardcoded IP addresses. CloudFront is an HTTP-based content delivery service and cannot handle UDP traffic. An Elastic IP address can be used only within a single Region and cannot be moved to and associated with a resource in another Region. The conditions that the clients cannot be changed and that UDP is required eliminate CloudFront and the DNS-based options.

prompt: An e-commerce company wants to replace 30 instances in an Auto Scaling group with a new AMI that has security patches applied. On weekday afternoons traffic is high, so service capacity must stay at 90% or more at all times, even during the replacement. The replacement must pause when 20% of the instances have been replaced and again when 50% have been replaced, so that the team can check metrics at each point. If an ALB 5xx alarm fires, the replacement must be stopped and rolled back to the previous configuration without human intervention. Version 2 of the launch template, which uses the new AMI, is ready, and the launch template $Latest version is frequently modified by another team. The on-call responder is not on standby at night, so the rollback decision must be made by the alarm alone, and user requests must continue to be processed during the replacement. All instances to be replaced belong to the same ALB target group and take about 3 minutes to warm up, and the deadline for deploying the security patch is this Friday. In the last manual replacement, some instances remained in service in an unhealthy state and caused an outage. An operations policy has been agreed that for the first 24 hours after deployment, the rollback decision is made by a single alarm only. Which solution BEST meets these requirements?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Start an instance refresh with a desired configuration that specifies the launch template at the fixed version number 2, and set a minimum healthy percentage of 90%, checkpoints at 20% and 50%, the 5xx alarm, and automatic rollback.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Without using an instance refresh, change the Auto Scaling group termination policy to OldestLaunchTemplate, and increase and then decrease the desired capacity so that instances from the old template are terminated first.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Start an instance refresh with the launch template version set to $Latest, set a minimum healthy percentage of 90% and checkpoints at 20% and 50%, and specify the 5xx alarm with automatic rollback enabled.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Start an instance refresh with a minimum healthy percentage of 90% but without checkpoints, and have a person check metrics; if there is a problem, cancel the refresh and start a new instance refresh again with the previous AMI.

explanation: The correct answer is to start an instance refresh with a desired configuration that specifies a fixed launch template version number, and to set up checkpoints and alarm-based automatic rollback. A minimum healthy percentage of 90% satisfies the capacity requirement, checkpoints pause at the 20% and 50% points to give a chance to validate, and when the alarm goes into ALARM, automatic rollback returns to the previous configuration. Rollback is available only when the refresh is started with a desired configuration specified, and it cannot be used with the $Latest or $Default version. A method that cancels manually without checkpoints requires human intervention and violates the requirement. Adjusting the termination policy has no stage-pause or rollback capability. The condition that another team frequently modifies $Latest means a fixed version number must be specified, and the condition that no one is on standby at night eliminates the manual cancellation approach.

prompt: The platform team pipeline at a retail group publishes the approved golden AMI ID every week to the AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store parameter /golden/al2023/ami in four Regions: Seoul, Tokyo, N. Virginia, and Ireland. The AWS CloudFormation templates of 12 development teams use hardcoded AMI IDs and per-Region Mappings, so the templates are edited every week. The company wants to make the templates Region-independent and have each stack update use the latest approved AMI. The AMI is published once a week and each team has a different stack update schedule, so there must be no procedure in which the template-owning teams check the AMI ID themselves. The platform team does not want to operate additional Lambda code or a new separate stack. The AMI publishing pipeline is owned by the platform team, and it has been agreed that the parameter name will not change. The CloudFormation execution role of each team already has the ssm:GetParameters permission, and the parameter is published in each Region in the same account. Each team updates its stack on its own schedule, so one team's update must not affect another team's stack. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST amount of change?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Build a pipeline that redeploys a template with updated Mappings AMI IDs to each Region every week by using StackSets, automating the template modification and deployment whenever the parameter changes.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Deploy a separate stack in each Region that exports the AMI ID as a stack output, and modify every team's templates to reference this value with Fn::ImportValue.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Add a Lambda-backed custom resource to the template that uses DescribeImages to look up the latest AMI with the approved tag and passes that ID as the ImageId of the launch template.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Declare the template parameter type as AWS::SSM::Parameter::Value<AWS::EC2::Image::Id> and set the default value to /golden/al2023/ami so that the parameter value in that Region is resolved when the stack is created and updated.

explanation: The correct answer is to use a template parameter of the SSM parameter type. The AWS::SSM::Parameter::Value<AWS::EC2::Image::Id> type retrieves the latest value from Parameter Store in that Region when the stack is created or updated, so Mappings are not needed and the template is Region-independent. Looking up the AMI with a custom resource requires maintaining Lambda code and implementing the tag rules yourself. Redeploying Mappings with StackSets requires automating template modification and still leaves per-Region values in the template. The export and import stacks require operating a separate stack in each Region and modifying every template, which is a large change. The conditions that there must be no procedure where teams check the AMI ID themselves and that no additional Lambda or stack is operated eliminate the custom resource and the export approach.

prompt: The platform team at a game company wants to delegate to a development organization of 200 developers the permission to create IAM roles for CI/CD directly. Roles created by the development teams must not be able to have permissions beyond the scope of Amazon S3, Amazon DynamoDB, and AWS Lambda, and the development teams must not be able to remove or modify the boundary policy. Dozens of roles are created per day, the security team has no staff to review individual roles, and only the security team must be able to change the boundary policy. Previously, roles were created through security team tickets, but this took two days on average and delayed deployments. The security team has already written a boundary policy that allows only common actions of S3, DynamoDB, and Lambda, and development team roles follow a convention of using the cicd- prefix. During audits, the company must be able to prove at once that a boundary is attached to any given role. This delegation applies only to the development account, and the security team keeps the permission to create roles in the production account as it does today. The development teams' CI/CD pipelines use AWS CodeBuild and Lambda deployments. The solution must operate as self-service without central approval. Which solution meets these requirements in the SAFEST way?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Grant the development teams AdministratorAccess, review the IAM Access Analyzer findings once a month, and find and delete roles with excessive permissions after the fact.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Receive all role creation requests as security team tickets, have the security team create the roles directly, and do not grant the development teams iam:* permissions.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Only set an IAM condition that requires the prefix in development team role names, and allow any managed policy to be attached as long as the prefix matches.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Allow CreateRole and policy attachment only when the specified boundary policy is attached by using the iam:PermissionsBoundary condition, and deny removal and modification of the boundary.

explanation: A delegation policy that enforces the permissions boundary condition is the correct answer. If role creation and policy attachment are allowed only when the specified boundary policy is attached through the iam:PermissionsBoundary condition, the effective permissions of a new role are always the intersection with the boundary, and denying the action that removes the boundary and the modification of the boundary policy closes the bypass. Granting administrator permissions and reviewing afterward is unsafe because excessive permissions exist in the meantime. Having the security team create roles directly conflicts with the self-service requirement without central approval. A prefix condition cannot limit the scope of permissions, so permissions beyond the boundary can be granted. Because a prefix cannot limit the scope of permissions, only the approach that enforces the boundary condition satisfies both the audit proof and self-service.

prompt: The development team at a media company wants to run unit tests every time a pull request in a GitHub repository is opened or updated and show the result as a status check on the PR. The scope is limited to PRs that target the main branch, and to reduce build costs the tests must run only when files under src/ change. The repository has an average of 30 PRs opened per day, and many PRs modify only documentation, so running a full build on every PR would waste a lot of build time. The company already uses AWS and has no staff to operate its own CI server. The team has 5 people and is considering moving to GitHub Actions next quarter, but this requirement must be handled right away. A Linux container is enough for the build environment, and the tests take 4 minutes on average. The repository is already connected to AWS through AWS CodeConnections, the branch protection rule requires passing status checks as a merge condition, and the company wants to avoid always-on infrastructure that incurs cost even when it is not in use. The development team has already agreed on the rule to skip builds for PRs that change only documentation, and a single src/ path rule is enough given the repository structure. Which solution meets these requirements in the MOST cost-effective way with the LEAST operational overhead?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Install Jenkins on Amazon EC2 to receive GitHub webhooks, configure a path filter plugin so that only changes under src/ are built, and publish build results to GitHub status checks with a plugin. The platform team manages patching and backups of the Jenkins server.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Create an AWS CodePipeline that runs on every push, runs the tests in CodeBuild after the source stage, and has an approver manually check the results in an approval stage before allowing the merge.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Use an Amazon EventBridge rule to run CodeBuild once a day to test all open PR branches in sequence, and email the results so that a person checks them.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Create a GitHub webhook on the CodeBuild project and specify a filter group for the PULL_REQUEST_CREATED and PULL_REQUEST_UPDATED events with BASE_REF set to main and FILE_PATH set to src/, and have the build status reported to the PR.

explanation: The correct answer is to use a CodeBuild GitHub webhook filter group. When BASE_REF and FILE_PATH filters are applied together to the PR creation and update events, a build starts only for PRs that target main and change src/. There is no server, cost is incurred only for the build time, and the status is reported to the PR. Jenkins violates the condition that the company has no staff to operate a CI server on its own. Running a pipeline on every push without path and branch conditions increases unnecessary builds and also requires manual checks. A once-a-day batch test does not meet the requirement to check every time a PR is opened or updated. The condition of avoiding always-on infrastructure eliminates Jenkins, and the requirement for per-PR status checks eliminates the nightly batch build.

prompt: The AWS Organizations organization of a logistics company consists of a management account and 80 member accounts. All member accounts are under the Workloads OU, and a few new accounts are created every month. The company wants the organization to use only the Seoul and N. Virginia Regions. Creating resources in other Regions must be blocked in all member accounts except the management account (including the root user), while calls to global services such as IAM, Route 53, and CloudFront must continue to work. It must also apply automatically to newly created accounts. Account administrators can modify the IAM policies in their own accounts, regulations prohibit data from being stored in unapproved Regions, and only the central security team must make changes. Currently no SCPs are attached other than FullAWSAccess, and the security team has exclusive permission to change SCPs in the management account. A previous audit found that a developer created a test database in an unapproved Region, and it was confirmed that no service is running outside the allowed Regions. Several teams in the organization already use global services such as CloudFront and IAM that are called only in specific Regions. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST amount of change?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Deploy an IAM policy that denies actions in Regions other than the two Regions to all member accounts by using StackSets, and have it attached to the users and roles in each account.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Attach to the Workloads OU an SCP that denies actions when aws:RequestedRegion is not an allowed Region, and use NotAction to exempt global service actions.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Attach a Region restriction policy as a permissions boundary to the IAM roles and users in each account, and check that the boundary is attached whenever a new role is created.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Detect resources created outside the allowed Regions with an AWS Config rule and configure an automatic remediation action to delete those resources.

explanation: A Region-deny SCP attached to the OU is the correct answer. An SCP is a ceiling that applies to all IAM principals in member accounts, including the root user, and when it is attached to an OU, new accounts inherit it automatically; the NotAction exception allows global services to continue to be used. An IAM policy deployed to accounts can be modified or detached by account administrators and does not apply to the root user. A permissions boundary must be attached to each role and user and has no effect on the root user, so gaps remain possible. Config remediation is a reactive response that deletes the resource after it has already been created, so it does not prevent creation itself. The condition that account administrators can change the IAM policies in their own accounts eliminates the IAM policy deployment approach.

prompt: An insurance company operates 40 development accounts under an OU managed by AWS Control Tower. In these accounts, developers repeatedly deploy unencrypted Amazon EBS volumes or Amazon S3 buckets that allow public read through AWS CloudFormation every quarter, which has led to audit findings. The security team wants to evaluate such resources at the stack operation stage before they are provisioned and fail the deployment if there is a violation. Approaches that detect or fix already-created resources after the fact are not acceptable, and the solution must be applied at the OU level without per-account configuration. Developers use the console in addition to CloudFormation, but this requirement is limited to CloudFormation deployments. Each development team has a different CI pipeline, so the security team cannot require each team to add a check stage, and the security team wants to manage rule changes in one place. There are two rules to enforce: required EBS encryption and a ban on S3 public read. The security team wants to check the control enablement history in the Control Tower console. It is enough for the evaluation result to be delivered immediately to developers as a deployment failure message. By regulation, changes to control enablement are approved by the security team, and the development teams do not have permission to disable controls. Which solution BEST meets these requirements?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Add a cfn-guard check stage to the CI pipelines of all development teams so that the pipeline fails if the template violates the rules, and have each team pull the rules file from a shared repository on its own.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Enable a detective control on the OU so that when an AWS Config rule finds a noncompliant resource, the finding is sent through Amazon EventBridge, and have the responsible person check the resource and delete it or encrypt it.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Turn on an AWS Config automatic remediation rule in each account of the OU so that when an unencrypted volume or a public bucket is found, AWS Systems Manager Automation replaces it with an encrypted volume and a private setting.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Enable an AWS Control Tower proactive control on the OU. Based on CloudFormation Hooks, it evaluates the resource configuration when a stack is created or updated and blocks the deployment if it is noncompliant.

explanation: The correct answer is a proactive control. Control Tower proactive controls are implemented with CloudFormation Hooks, so they evaluate the configuration before resources are created or changed by a stack operation, and when enabled on an OU they apply to all accounts in that OU. Detective controls find already-created resources after the fact through Config rules, which violates the requirement for pre-provisioning evaluation. Automatic remediation rules are also a reactive action that fixes resources after they are created. A cfn-guard check in CI verifies only deployments that go through the pipeline and requires per-team setup, so it does not meet the requirement for OU-wide uniform application. The condition that each team has a different pipeline and a check stage cannot be enforced eliminates the cfn-guard approach.

prompt: A manufacturing group wants to view the metrics and log groups of 40 source accounts in its organization from a central monitoring account without switching accounts. The source accounts span 3 OUs, and a few new accounts are added to the OUs every month, and the new accounts should be included automatically. The company will not build a pipeline that replicates the data separately (because of replication cost and latency), and the operations team wants to view metrics, log groups, and AWS X-Ray traces in a single console. Source account administrators must not be given access to the monitoring account, and source accounts may choose which data types to share only within the scope set by the monitoring account. The workloads in both the monitoring account and the source accounts are in the Seoul Region, and source account administrators continue to manage the metrics and log groups of their own accounts directly. The operations team in the monitoring account must not be able to modify resources in the source accounts. The operations team wants additional cost to be minimal and wants the newly created resources to be limited to one in the monitoring account and one per source account. The retention period of the log groups that the operations team views follows the source account's setting as is. Which TWO configurations meet these requirements? (Select TWO.)

choices.label: A
choices.text: Each source account creates a link within the range of types allowed by the monitoring account, and uses a CloudFormation template for OU-level deployment.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Create one sink in each source account, and have the monitoring account create a link to each sink to pull the data.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Create a subscription filter for each log group in each source account that sends logs to a log group in the monitoring account, and replicate metrics by using Metric Streams to collect them.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Create a sink in the monitoring account and use the sink policy to allow accounts in the organization or in the target OUs to create links.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Even if a source account chooses to share trace types that the monitoring account did not allow, only the allowed types are shared and link creation succeeds.

explanation: The correct answers are the sink and sink policy in the monitoring account, and the link that each source account creates within the allowed scope. The sink is the connection point in the monitoring account and the link is managed by the source account; using Organizations and a CloudFormation template means new accounts are onboarded automatically. Subscription filters and Metric Streams are separate pipelines that replicate data, which conflicts with the requirements. If a source account selects more types than the monitoring account allows, link creation fails and nothing is shared. A sink is a resource placed once per Region in the monitoring account and is not created in each source account. The condition that no data replication pipeline is built eliminates the subscription filter approach, and the condition that the source account decides the scope of sharing eliminates E.

prompt: A central operations team at an online education company wants to receive AWS Health scheduled events (such as EC2 instance retirement) occurring across all 60 accounts in its organization as a single feed, and respond with Amazon SNS notifications and AWS Systems Manager Automation. The organization has all features enabled and uses a Business or higher Support plan. Currently each account owner receives notifications by email and often misses them, and last month an instance scheduled for retirement was stopped as is. The response staff can access only the operations account, this operations account can be designated as the AWS Health delegated administrator, and when a retirement schedule is announced, the instance must be replaced within 7 days. The target events focus on EC2 instance retirement notifications, and the notifications are delivered through an SNS topic to the operations team's chat channel. The Automation runbook in the operations account already implements the instance replacement procedure, and events must arrive for accounts added to the organization later without separate configuration. The operations team has 5 people and must be able to check the handling records per account in case handling of retirement notifications is delayed. Which TWO configurations meet these requirements without creating rules in each account and without operating custom-built polling code? (Select TWO.)

choices.label: A
choices.text: Receive AWS Trusted Advisor check results as a weekly report and have the responsible person manually check whether any instances are scheduled for retirement.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Have a Lambda function in the central account assume a role in each account, query the Health API for new events every minute, and publish the results to Amazon SNS.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Enable AWS Health organizational view in the management account and, if needed, designate a delegated administrator account.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Use StackSets to deploy to all 60 accounts a rule that matches aws.health events and a cross-account event bus target so that all rules forward to the event bus in the operations account.

choices.label: E
choices.text: In the management account or the delegated administrator account, create a rule that matches aws.health events and set Amazon SNS and Automation as targets.

explanation: The correct answers are enabling the Health organizational view and an EventBridge rule in the management account or the delegated administrator account. When the organizational view is turned on, the management account or the delegated administrator account receives the Health events of the entire organization as a single feed, so you only need to place one rule there and connect it to Amazon SNS and SSM Automation. Deploying rules and delivery targets to each account creates configuration in 60 places even though a single feed exists, which conflicts with the requirements. Assuming a role in each account and a 1-minute polling Lambda function involve custom-built code and invocation cost. A weekly Trusted Advisor report requires a person to check it and cannot automatically handle scheduled events immediately. The condition that events must arrive for new accounts without configuration eliminates deploying rules to each account.

prompt: An advertising platform needs to receive an alarm when the memory utilization of a JVM application running in an Auto Scaling group (up to 60 instances) exceeds 80%. Instances are replaced dozens of times a day because of scale-in and scale-out, so per-instance alarms are hard to maintain, and the team wants to view the group average as a single metric. The default EC2 metrics do not include memory utilization. A memory threshold breach must be detected within 5 minutes, and the alarm configuration must be managed as code (IaC). The team already deploys the CloudWatch agent configuration through Systems Manager in the launch template, so changing the agent configuration is not a burden. The CloudWatch agent starts automatically at boot through the launch template user data, and metrics are collected at 60-second intervals in the CWAgent namespace. The metric used for the alarm must be aggregated by the group name dimension rather than by instance ID. The alarm should fire when the group's average memory stays above 80% for 5 minutes or more, and individual instance notifications are not needed. Which configuration BEST meets these requirements while minimizing the number of alarms and management tasks?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Collect mem_used_percent with the agent, create a group-level metric by using AutoScalingGroupName dimension aggregation (aggregation_dimensions), and create the alarm on it.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Create an alarm that aggregates the default EC2 metric MemoryUtilization at the Auto Scaling group level, and automatically update the alarm targets when instances are replaced.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Have each instance send the result of the free command to PutMetricData with cron, and have a Lambda function create and delete alarms per instance ID.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Turn on Auto Scaling group metrics collection and create an alarm on a group metric such as GroupInServiceInstances as a proxy for memory utilization.

explanation: Memory collection by the agent and a group-level aggregation dimension is the correct answer. If the agent collects mem_used_percent and aggregates it with the AutoScalingGroupName dimension, one alarm on a single group metric is enough even when instances change. The default EC2 metrics do not include memory, so an approach that uses a default metric called MemoryUtilization does not work. Adding a Lambda function that creates alarms to a cron and PutMetricData script introduces custom-built code and lifecycle management of per-instance alarms, which is a heavy burden. Group metrics are instance counts and capacity information and are unrelated to memory utilization. The condition that instances are replaced dozens of times a day eliminates the per-instance alarm configuration.

prompt: The automated account security remediation at a fintech company works by having an Amazon EventBridge rule deliver events to a Lambda function that fixes violating resources. Sometimes this Lambda function fails to receive events because of temporary throttling and permission errors that occur during deployments. If such an event is lost, remediation is missed, and missed remediation becomes an audit finding, so the company wants to store failed events and reprocess them after the cause is resolved. The existing rule structure and Lambda code must not be changed, and additional development must be minimal. Events occur only in the Region where the rule is located, and there must be no loss during the retention period. The affected Lambda function identifies remediation targets by tags and is written to be idempotent, so reprocessing the same event has no side effects. The default retry settings of the rule target are kept as they are. This rule processes several thousand events per day on average, and one event corresponds to exactly one violating resource. The company wants to confirm that no events were lost by checking the number of messages that accumulate in the queue. Which of the options available in the rule target settings is MOST appropriate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Specify an Amazon SQS standard queue in the same Region as the target dead-letter queue (DLQ) and attach a queue policy that allows EventBridge to call SendMessage.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Specify an Amazon SQS FIFO queue as the DLQ of the rule target to guarantee the order of failed events, and reprocess the messages accumulated in the queue with Lambda.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Specify an Amazon SQS standard queue that was already created in a different Region as the DLQ, extending to a multi-Region configuration so that failed events are stored even during a Regional failure.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Only set an alarm on the FailedInvocations metric of the rule target and, when the alarm fires, have the responsible person manually recreate and resend the event.

explanation: Specifying an SQS standard queue in the same Region as the DLQ is the correct configuration. Errors that cannot be resolved by retrying, such as permission errors, go to the DLQ right away without retries, and later reprocessing the queue messages after fixing the cause means no event is lost; the queue policy must allow EventBridge to call SendMessage. EventBridge DLQs support only standard queues, so a FIFO queue cannot be specified. The DLQ queue must be in the same Region as the rule, so a queue in another Region cannot be used. A metric alarm only tells you about the failure and does not store the event itself, so there is no data to reprocess. The alarm-only approach cannot store the events and therefore does not satisfy the requirement to prevent loss.

prompt: A healthcare SaaS company pushes container images to Amazon ECR and runs them on Amazon ECS for months at a time. There were no problems at push time, but a CVE disclosed afterward can introduce new CRITICAL vulnerabilities in already deployed images. The company wants to detect such cases without a separate rescan job and send a notification to the security team's SNS topic whenever an active CRITICAL finding appears. The ECR repository holds hundreds of images, and the deployment pipeline is owned by another team and cannot be modified. When a new CVE is disclosed, the company needs to know which images are affected as soon as possible. The security team has 3 people and does not have the capacity to build and maintain a scan schedule on its own. The ECS services are spread across 5 accounts, but the images are stored in a central registry in the Seoul Region. The security team wants to receive only CRITICAL vulnerabilities as immediate notifications and review the rest on a dashboard. Dozens of new production images are pushed per month on average, and old images also remain in service for long periods. The notification must include the image name, tag, and vulnerability ID so that the responder can act right away. Which solution has the LEAST operational overhead?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Turn on scan on push with ECR basic scanning, and create a schedule in which a Lambda function calls StartImageScan for all images in the repository every day.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Turn on Amazon Inspector continuous scanning for ECR, and send CRITICAL, ACTIVE Inspector2 finding events to Amazon SNS with an EventBridge rule.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Turn on Amazon GuardDuty and receive runtime threat detection findings as notifications to stand in for detecting newly introduced vulnerabilities in images.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Add a vulnerability scanner to the AWS CodeBuild image build stage and, if the build-time result is clean, do not scan again afterward.

explanation: Inspector continuous scanning with an event rule is the correct answer. Continuous scanning rescans images not only when a new image is pushed but also when a related CVE is added to the Inspector database, and new findings and status changes are emitted to EventBridge, so you only need to connect the CRITICAL, ACTIVE condition to SNS. Basic scanning runs at push time or as a manual scan, so you would have to build and maintain a daily rescan Lambda function yourself. GuardDuty is a threat detection service and does not inspect an image's package vulnerabilities. Checking only at build time misses CVEs disclosed afterward. The conditions that the deployment pipeline cannot be modified and that there is no capacity to build a scan schedule eliminate scan on push and the build-stage scan.

prompt: A fintech company wants to track, per service, a latency objective of "99% of requests within 300 ms" and the error budget burn rate for 30 microservices running on Amazon EKS, and wants to receive alarms when the burn rate is high. The service teams use a mix of Java, Python, and Node.js and have different deployment schedules, so code changes cannot be coordinated at the same time. Changes to service code must be minimized, and the company also wants to avoid managing formulas that calculate objective attainment by hand. The objectives must be managed at the service and operation level, and metrics and traces are already collected in Amazon CloudWatch and AWS X-Ray. The SRE team has only 2 people. Calls between services use a mix of gRPC and HTTP, and the EKS cluster already collects metrics with Container Insights. The company wants to view the error budget burn rate over two windows, 1 hour and 6 hours, and executives receive a quarterly per-service report on a monthly 99.9% availability objective. Introducing a service mesh or sidecars is not on this quarter's roadmap, and the current configuration must be kept as is. Which solution BEST meets these requirements?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Use CloudWatch Application Signals to automatically instrument the services on Amazon EKS, create latency SLOs per service and operation, and then set burn rate alarms.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Create a TargetResponseTime p99 alarm on the ALB target group for each service, and calculate the error budget burn rate yourself with dashboard metric math.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Add PutMetricData calls to each service's code to publish latency yourself, calculate attainment and budget burn with metric math, and set alarms.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Raise AWS X-Ray sampling to 100% and turn on X-Ray Insights notifications to track latency SLO violations and error budget burn.

explanation: Application Signals SLOs are the correct answer. Application Signals automatically collects Latency and Availability metrics for services and operations and lets you create SLOs and set alarms on attainment and error budget burn rate (burn rate), so code changes and formula management are small. An ALB response time alarm has no objectives or budget concept at the level of operations inside a service, so you would have to write the formulas yourself. Adding PutMetricData to the code would require modifying 30 services. X-Ray Insights is anomaly detection and does not define target values or an error budget, and 100% sampling only increases cost. The requirement for objectives and burn rate at the service and operation level cannot be met by ALB metrics or X-Ray alone.

prompt: The web tier of a video streaming company needs 6 instances during peak hours. At peak, one instance handles one-sixth of the total load and has no spare CPU headroom. The service must run without a capacity shortage during peak hours even if one entire Availability Zone in the Seoul Region fails, and when one zone disappears, the remaining instances must handle the entire peak load. Normal-time cost must be as low as possible. The Auto Scaling group distributes instances evenly across multiple Availability Zones, and the instance type and size are fixed. A design that assumes new capacity can be obtained in time after a failure occurs is not allowed. The service runs On-Demand, and reserved capacity contracts are outside the scope of this review. All instances are stateless servers built from the same AMI, subnets exist in all three AZs, and the Application Load Balancer also spans three AZs. This question asks for the minimum capacity during peak hours, and a failure of one AZ is assumed to be a situation in which all instances in that AZ disappear at the same time. The instance type of the Auto Scaling group is fixed, subnet capacity in each AZ is sufficient, and instances are not concentrated in a single AZ. Which configuration meets these requirements MOST cost-effectively?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Keep 6 instances in each of 2 Availability Zones, for a total of 12 instances, as the minimum capacity during peak hours.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Keep 3 instances in each of 3 Availability Zones, for a total of 9 instances, as the minimum capacity during peak hours.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Keep 2 instances in each of 3 Availability Zones, for a total of 6 instances, and accept that CPU utilization of the remaining 4 instances rises when one zone disappears.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Keep 3 instances in each of 2 Availability Zones, for a total of 6 instances, and leave it to Auto Scaling to fill the capacity in the remaining zone when a failure occurs.

explanation: The correct answer is 3 instances in each of 3 Availability Zones, for a total of 9. Even if one zone disappears, 6 instances remain in the other two zones, which satisfies the peak capacity, and for static stability the design does not depend on obtaining new capacity during a failure. A configuration with 6 instances in each of 2 zones, 12 in total, also satisfies the requirement but has 3 more instances and is less cost-effective. Keeping 3 instances in each of 2 zones, 6 in total, and leaving it to Auto Scaling after a failure drops capacity to 3 instances right after the failure, and scaling is a control plane operation that depends on obtaining new capacity, which violates the constraint. With 2 instances in each of 3 zones, 6 in total, only 4 instances remain when one zone disappears, which does not satisfy the peak capacity of 6. Under the condition that reserved capacity contracts are not under review, the configuration that increases the number of AZs to reduce the total number of instances is the cheapest.

prompt: In a SaaS organization, 5 to 10 new accounts are created every week. The security team wants to automate, without human intervention, enabling Amazon GuardDuty and deploying an IAM role for auditing in each new account. It wants to use a delegated administrator and AWS CloudFormation for the service settings. A new account must have the same security baseline within minutes of creation, and the product teams that create accounts have no permission to configure security settings. The organization has all features enabled, and the accounts are spread across 3 OUs. Currently two security team members configure accounts manually by following a checklist, and omissions keep recurring. Both settings are for the Seoul Region, and new accounts are created with the Organizations CreateAccount API rather than AWS Control Tower. The IAM role for auditing is defined in a single template, and the security team has already designated a delegated administrator account. The platform team is responsible for creating new accounts, but afterward the security settings must be aligned automatically according to the security team's policy. Which TWO configurations meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead? (Select TWO.)

choices.label: A
choices.text: Create an AWS Config aggregator at the organization level, and GuardDuty and the audit role are automatically installed in new accounts.

choices.label: B
choices.text: In the GuardDuty delegated administrator account, turn on the organization's auto-enable setting so that GuardDuty is automatically enabled in new member accounts.

choices.label: C
choices.text: When a new account is created, have the responsible person log in to the account, turn on GuardDuty, and deploy the stack directly by following the checklist.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Target the organization OUs with service-managed StackSets and turn on automatic deployment so that the audit role stack is automatically deployed to new accounts.

choices.label: E
choices.text: If the SCP allows the guardduty:CreateDetector action, GuardDuty is automatically turned on in new accounts and the role is also created.

explanation: The correct answers are the GuardDuty organization auto-enable setting and StackSets automatic deployment. The auto-enable setting of the delegated administrator turns on GuardDuty for new member accounts, and automatic deployment of service-managed StackSets deploys the role stack to new accounts that join the OU. An SCP does not grant permissions or turn on services and only sets a ceiling. A Config aggregator is a feature that collects configuration and compliance data and does not install other services. Manual work following a checklist requires human intervention, which conflicts with the automation requirement and with minimizing operational overhead. The conditions that the product teams have no permission to configure security settings and that the work must be handled without human intervention eliminate the checklist approach.

prompt: On a payment platform, when a database failure occurs, more than 20 alarms for application server error rate, response latency, and queue backlog go into ALARM at the same time, and dozens of Amazon SNS text messages are sent to the on-call engineer. The cause is the same, and separate database alarms that watch the DB instance CPU and connection count already exist; the engineer wants to be paged only once when the database is actually abnormal. The individual alarm metrics must be kept as they are, and detection latency must not increase. The on-call rotation must page only one person at a time, and the alarm history must continue to be retained per individual metric for post-incident analysis. The configuration must stay simple even when new services are added, and the company does not want to operate separate code for deduplicating notifications. The 20 or so alarms are owned by different teams and each has its own SNS topic, but on-call receives pages only through one topic connected to the paging service. The composite alarm rule must be able to express a combination of the database alarm and multiple service alarms. The on-call engineer wants to know immediately from a single alarm which component is the cause, and the database abnormality is already defined by two alarms. Which solution meets the requirements MOST appropriately?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Increase the evaluation period and the number of data points of all alarms so that transient alarms are not mixed in, reducing the number of alarms that fire at the same time.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Apply a filter policy to the SNS subscription so that only the first of the messages arriving in the same time window is delivered to the on-call engineer.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Set the composite alarm rule to fire when both the database alarm and the application error rate alarm are in ALARM, and remove the SNS actions from the child alarms so that only the composite alarm pages.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Receive alarm state change events through Amazon EventBridge, have a Lambda function record them in Amazon DynamoDB to deduplicate, and then publish only one message to Amazon SNS.

explanation: A composite alarm is the correct answer. A composite alarm evaluates the states of other alarms with AND and OR, so the individual metrics and evaluation settings can stay as they are while paging comes from only one place, the composite alarm. Increasing the evaluation period conflicts with the constraint on detection latency and still leaves the problem of many alarms firing. An SNS filter policy is a message attribute matching feature and cannot deduplicate by time window or by cause. Implementing your own deduplication with EventBridge, Lambda, and DynamoDB requires maintaining code and a state store, so it has the highest operational overhead. The condition that the individual alarm metrics and evaluation settings are kept and detection latency must not increase eliminates extending the evaluation period.

prompt: The security team of a retail group wants to centrally close, in one operation, security group rules that open inbound port 22 to 0.0.0.0/0 across 3 OUs (45 accounts) and 3 Regions of the organization. Applying the change to all accounts at once carries a risk of outage, so the number of account and Region locations running at the same time must be limited, and the run must stop if errors exceed 10%. The company wants to take the list of target accounts from the organization and does not want to edit the list by hand when accounts are added. The execution history must be viewable centrally in one place, and access must use only temporary credentials without creating long-term credentials in each account. The security team has 4 people and cannot spend time developing one-off scripts. The execution roles that Automation will assume have already been deployed to the 45 target accounts with StackSets, and the only rules to remove are those with port 22 open to 0.0.0.0/0, regardless of tags. The work is carried out outside business hours, and some accounts with restricted access may fail. The results are included in an organization-wide audit report, so success and failure per account and Region must remain in the execution history. Which solution is MOST appropriate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Share the runbook with each account administrator, have them run it themselves in each account on a set date, and collect completion status in a spreadsheet.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Run a script that iterates over 45 account profiles using long-term IAM user access keys from the management account and removes the rules with the AWS CLI.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Run the revoke-security-group-ingress command on each EC2 instance with Run Command, and add security group modification permissions to the instance profiles.

choices.label: D
choices.text: From the delegated administrator account, run SSM Automation across multiple accounts and Regions targeting the OUs, and set concurrency and an error threshold.

explanation: Multi-account and multi-Region Automation is the correct answer. If you target the OUs from the central account, the account list is expanded from the organization, and location concurrency and the error threshold control the rollout speed and stop conditions (deploying the execution roles in the target accounts with StackSets is the recommended method). Manual execution per account has no controllable concurrency or error threshold and requires people to handle 45 accounts. A long-term access key script carries a key exposure risk and requires building concurrency control code yourself. A security group is an account and Region level resource, not something inside an instance, so Run Command does not fit and only needlessly broadens the instance profile permissions. The execution roles are already deployed, so the prerequisite for multi-account Automation is met, and running manually per account does not satisfy the concurrency and error threshold requirements.

prompt: The order service of a global SaaS stores order data in Amazon Aurora MySQL and session data in an Amazon DynamoDB table in the Seoul Region. The company wants to use the Osaka Region as disaster recovery (DR) in case the entire Seoul Region fails. The requirements are to limit data loss to a few seconds, to make the DR Region writable within minutes during a failure, and to have no recovery step that takes long, such as restoring from a snapshot. The Osaka Region normally receives no write load, and the company also wants to automate the recovery procedure and run regular DR drills. The order database is about 2 TB and there are 2 DBAs, so managed features are preferred over building and monitoring replication setups by hand. The Aurora cluster in Seoul already has a read replica in the same Region, and the Osaka Region has a VPC and application AMIs ready, so only the connection endpoint needs to change during recovery. DR failover automation is handled as a separate task. Recovery drills are held every six months, and drills must not affect the service in the Seoul Region. Which TWO components meet these requirements? (Select TWO.)

choices.label: A
choices.text: Add an Aurora read replica in another Availability Zone in the Seoul Region, and when a failure occurs, promote this replica so that the application in the Osaka Region connects to it.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Configure the session table as a DynamoDB global table, add a replica in the Osaka Region, and have the Osaka replica receive reads and writes as is when a failure occurs.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Configure the Aurora database as an Aurora global database, add a secondary cluster in Osaka, and promote and use the secondary cluster when a failure occurs.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Turn on continuous backups for the DynamoDB table, and when a failure occurs, run a point-in-time restore in the Osaka Region to create a new table and have the application use that table.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Copy Aurora cluster snapshots to the Osaka Region every hour with AWS Backup, and when a failure occurs, restore a new cluster from a snapshot to resume the service.

explanation: The correct answers are an Aurora global database and a DynamoDB global table. An Aurora global database uses dedicated storage-level infrastructure to replicate to the secondary Region, typically with latency under 1 second, and the secondary cluster can be promoted during a failure, which satisfies data loss of a few seconds and a fast writable state. A DynamoDB global table replicates continuously across Regions, so the Osaka replica can receive reads and writes right away. Copying snapshots and restoring takes a long time to restore and has a data loss window measured in hours, which violates the requirements. A point-in-time restore also takes time to create a new table. A read replica in the same Region does not help with a failure of the entire Region. The background that a read replica already exists in the same Region does not protect against a Regional failure, so it does not change the judgment of the correct answer.

prompt: An AWS CodePipeline pipeline in the shared services account of a game company stores build artifacts in the pipeline artifact bucket and deploys them to an AWS CodeDeploy application in the production account. The pipeline must be operated in only one place, the shared services account (so that approval history and audit logs can be viewed in one place). The artifact bucket is currently encrypted with the default AWS managed key (aws/s3), and the deploy action in the production account fails because it cannot read the artifacts. The artifacts may include production configuration files, so approaches that open the bucket to the outside or weaken encryption will not pass the security review. The production account must not access resources in the shared services account other than the CodeDeploy permissions that the deployment will exercise. Builds run in AWS CodeBuild in the Seoul Region, and the CodeDeploy deployment group in the production account is already prepared. Production account administrators must not be able to change the pipeline configuration in the shared services account, and deployments happen three or four times a day. The pipeline's approval stages and deployment history are retained in one place, the shared services account, for audit purposes. Which actions are needed to meet this requirement in a safe way that grants only the permissions needed in the production account? (Select TWO.)

choices.label: A
choices.text: Create in the production account a cross-account role that the pipeline service role can assume, grant it CodeDeploy permissions and access to the artifact bucket and the KMS key, and specify it as the roleArn of the deploy action.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Add a statement that allows the production account root to the key policy of the aws/s3 AWS managed key so that the production account can decrypt the artifacts with the same managed key, and leave the bucket policy and the cross-account role unchanged.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Create a separate CodePipeline in the production account that subscribes to the source repository in the shared services account, replace the artifact bucket with a new bucket owned by the production account, run the pipelines in both accounts in parallel, and manage deployment history separately per account.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Disable encryption on the artifact bucket and allow s3:GetObject to the entire production account in the bucket policy so that anyone in the production account can read the artifact objects without key permissions, and do not create a separate role.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Replace the artifact store encryption key with a customer managed KMS key in the shared services account, grant usage permissions to the service role and the production account, and allow the production account role to read through the bucket policy.

explanation: The correct answers are to have the production account read the artifacts by using a customer managed KMS key and a bucket policy, and to create a cross-account role in the production account that the pipeline service role assumes. An AWS managed key has a key policy that cannot be changed, so it cannot be shared with another account, which means a customer managed key is required, and cross-account access works only when both the key policy and the bucket policy allow the other account. The deploy action assumes the production account role to call CodeDeploy and access the bucket and the key. Adding the production account to the managed key policy does not work because the policy cannot be modified. Turning off encryption and opening read access to the entire account is excessive permission that breaks the principle of least privilege. Putting a separate pipeline in the production account violates the constraint that the pipeline is operated in only one account. The condition that production account administrators must not be able to change the pipeline also supports keeping the pipeline in the single shared services account.

prompt: An e-commerce company remediates, with an AWS Systems Manager Automation runbook, RDS instances that an AWS Config rule detects as publicly accessible. Instances tagged Env=prod may have connection drops during remediation, so remediation must run only after one of two approvers approves, while other environments must be remediated automatically right away. The solution runs in a single account, and the company wants to minimize custom code. The approval request must be delivered to the responsible people through Amazon SNS, instances that are not prod must be remediated immediately without waiting for approval, and the approval wait time must not exceed one day. The operations team has 3 people and cannot develop a new approval system, and the Config automatic remediation configuration is already in use in the development environment. The remediation runbook changes the PubliclyAccessible attribute of an RDS instance to false, and prod instances experience a brief connection drop. The two approvers are specified as IAM roles, and there are many non-prod instances, so approval requests piling up would be a problem. The runbook is already written as an SSM document, and the only parts to be changed are the approval step and the branching setup. Which solution is MOST appropriate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Exclude prod instances from Config automatic remediation, have the responsible person who receives the noncompliance notification through Amazon SNS turn off public access manually in the console, and configure automatic remediation only for the other non-prod environments.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Develop your own approval system in which a remediation Lambda function puts an approval request message into Amazon SQS and polls for the responder's reply, call it from Config remediation, and handle the response deadline and the verification of the number of approvers in code.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Use an IAM policy condition to deny the modify action of the remediation role on resources tagged prod so that remediation does not run without approval, and after approval have the responsible person lift the policy separately.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Use aws:branch so that only when the Env tag is prod it goes through aws:approve (2 approvers, minimum 1 approval, timeout 86400 seconds), and attach this runbook to Config automatic remediation.

explanation: A runbook that uses aws:branch and aws:approve is the correct answer. aws:approve pauses Automation until a designated approver approves and announces the request through Amazon SNS, and because the default timeout is 7 days, the one-day limit is met by setting the timeout to 86400 seconds. If the branch applies the approval only to prod, other environments are remediated immediately without waiting for approval, which meets the requirements without code. Excluding prod from automatic remediation and handling it manually removes the flow in which remediation runs automatically after approval and increases the responsible person's work. An SQS approval system requires custom development and maintenance. An IAM deny condition only makes remediation fail and provides no path to run it after approval. The condition that there are many non-prod instances and approval waits cannot be applied to them puts the approach of requiring approval for all remediation at a disadvantage.

prompt: The website of an e-commerce company runs on 24 Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group behind an Application Load Balancer. During in-place deployments, some instances served a mix of the old and new versions, which repeatedly caused problems. The company wants to prepare the new version fully on separate instances and then switch over at once at the ALB, and during the hour after deployment it must be possible to immediately roll back to the old-version instances if a problem is found. After 1 hour, the previous instances must be cleaned up to save cost. During the Black Friday period, a failed deployment means lost revenue, so rollback must not take longer than a few minutes. The team already uses AWS CodeDeploy as its deployment tool and has no staff to maintain separate deployment scripts. Target groups can be used on the ALB for blue and green, the deployment artifacts are in Amazon S3, and the CodeDeploy agent is installed on all instances. New instances created by scale-out during the deployment must also receive the same version. The pre-deployment check is already implemented with a CodeDeploy hook and does not need to be built again. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Use a CodeDeploy EC2 blue/green deployment to copy the Auto Scaling group and create a replacement environment, reroute traffic all at once, and specify in the deployment group settings that the original instances are terminated after waiting 60 minutes.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Use a CodeDeploy in-place deployment with the HalfAtATime configuration, perform a manual rollback that redeploys the previous revision if a problem is found, and keep using the instances without replacing them.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Create a new Auto Scaling group and target group with AWS CloudFormation for every deployment, write a script that changes the ALB listener rule, and add a scheduled Lambda function that deletes the previous group after 1 hour.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Change the launch template version of the existing Auto Scaling group to the new AMI, run an instance refresh with a minimum healthy percentage of 100%, and use instance refresh rollback if there is a problem, even after completion.

explanation: CodeDeploy EC2 blue/green deployment is the correct answer. The entire replacement environment is prepared first and switched over at once, so versions are not mixed, and specifying that the original instances terminate after waiting 60 minutes allows an immediate rollback to the old environment during that time and automatic cleanup afterward. An in-place deployment replaces instances sequentially, so the version mixing problem remains and rollback requires a redeployment. Building it yourself with CloudFormation and Lambda is possible but requires maintaining scripts and cleanup tasks yourself. An instance refresh can be rolled back only while it is in progress and cannot be rolled back after completion, and versions are also mixed during replacement. The condition that there is no staff to maintain separate deployment scripts eliminates the self-built stack replacement approach.

prompt: At a consumer lending company, multiple teams create hundreds of log groups, and some logs contain data in the form of card numbers and Korean resident registration numbers. The company must mask this data at ingestion time in all log groups, including those created in the future, and allow viewing of the original data only for the security audit role. Development teams can create log groups freely, and ordinary developers who read the logs must not be allowed access to the original data. The masking results are used for compliance reporting, so there must be no per-team configuration omissions. The log ingestion paths (agents, Lambda, containers) differ by team, so the ingestion-side code cannot be modified. The log groups exist only in the Seoul Region, and each team has a different retention period and encryption key. The security team wants to manage, in one place, the policy that defines which data types to mask. The security audit role is attached to only a few security staff, and viewing of the original data is allowed only at the time of an audit. Card numbers appear in the logs in a 16-digit format, and Korean resident registration numbers appear in a format that includes a hyphen. Which solution has the LEAST operational overhead?

choices.label: A
