choices.text: Build a script that attaches a data protection policy to each log group, run it with Amazon EventBridge when a new log group is created to add the policy, and have the responsible team reattach the policy on log groups where the run failed.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Apply a subscription filter to all log groups so that a Lambda function writes a copy with sensitive values masked to a new log group, set a short retention period on the original log groups so that they are deleted automatically, and let ordinary developers read only the copies.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Specify in an account-level data protection policy a managed data identifier for card numbers and a custom data identifier that defines the Korean resident registration number format with a regular expression, and grant the logs:Unmask permission only to the security audit role.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Encrypt the log groups with a customer managed KMS key, allow only the security audit role to decrypt with the key policy so that ordinary users cannot see the original data, and configure every new log group to be associated with the same key.

explanation: An account-level data protection policy is the correct answer. An account policy applies to both existing log groups and log groups created in the future, card numbers are matched by a managed data identifier, and Korean resident registration numbers, which are not in the managed list, are defined with a regular-expression-based custom data identifier and masked together. Masked data is hidden at ingestion time, and only principals with the logs:Unmask permission can see the original. A per-log-group script leaves a gap between the creation of a new group and the attachment of the policy, and the code must also be maintained. A subscription filter with a Lambda copy stores the original data in the source log group and requires operating a pipeline yourself. KMS encryption protects data at rest and cannot mask at the field level. The condition that the ingestion paths differ by team so code cannot be modified and the condition that log groups created in the future must be included support the account-level policy.

prompt: An order processing company uses a local sampling rule JSON file of the AWS X-Ray SDK for its order service running on 120 Amazon EC2 instances. Each instance samples independently, so the total amount recorded is larger than expected and trace storage costs have grown. The /checkout path must be kept at a high rate for incident analysis and all other paths at a low rate, and the company does not want to redeploy code every time the rules change. The trace storage volume must be reduced to one-third or less of the current volume, and /checkout requests must be traced without exception during incident analysis. Instances scale in and out frequently, and the company does not want a procedure that separately deploys a rule file whenever a new instance starts. The service is written in Java, and the X-Ray SDK and daemon are installed on all instances. The current local rule is a fixed rate of 5%, and high-volume paths such as the search API are recorded at the same rate, so most traces have low value. The payments team wants all /checkout calls to be recorded. Trace storage cost is increasing noticeably on the monthly bill, and the finance team has asked for a reduction plan by next quarter. Which solution BEST meets these requirements?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Add a /checkout entry to the local JSON rule and redeploy it to all 120 instances, and afterward repeat the redeployment and restart in the same way every time the rate changes.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Create an X-Ray group and include only /checkout requests in the filter expression, so that traces not belonging to the group are not recorded and cost is reduced.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Record all traces but shorten the X-Ray data retention period to lower storage cost, and query only /checkout when needed.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Define sampling rules in the X-Ray service (with a high priority for the /checkout rule) and configure remote sampling so that the library reads the service's rules.

explanation: Service-side sampling rules with remote sampling are the correct answer. When rules are placed in X-Ray, the service distributes the reservoir to instances as per-instance quotas, so the combined recorded volume does not balloon, a higher-priority /checkout rule can set its own rate, and changes do not require redeployment. A local JSON file samples independently per instance, so the reservoirs add up and changes require redeployment. A group is a feature for filtering stored traces and does not change the amount recorded. Recording everything increases cost, and the X-Ray retention period is not an item that users can shorten to save cost. The condition that the company does not want to deploy a rule file separately to new instances eliminates the local JSON approach.

prompt: A real estate platform runs a manually created Amazon S3 bucket and Amazon DynamoDB table in production, and data has already accumulated (tens of TB in the bucket, hundreds of millions of items in the table). These two resources must be brought under the management of a new AWS CloudFormation stack without deletion or re-creation. The template defines properties that match the current configuration of both resources. The service must not be interrupted during the import, and no resource replacement must occur if the template is changed right after the import. The infrastructure team wants to change these resources only through code from now on, and has neither the time nor the budget to copy data. Both resources are in the Seoul Region and do not belong to any other CloudFormation stack. Properties such as encryption and versioning are defined in the template with the same values as the current ones, and the work will be done in a weekend maintenance window, but applications that read and write both resources must keep running. After the work, the names and ARNs of the two resources must not change because other teams already reference these ARNs in their configuration. Which actions are needed to import them safely so that no data is lost? (Select TWO.)

choices.label: A
choices.text: Copy the data of the existing bucket and table to new resources created from the template, then delete the originals and reuse the names so that the new resources take the place of the originals.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Create a change set of the import type for the stack, specify each resource's identifier value (bucket name, table name), and run the change set to associate the existing resources with the logical IDs in the template.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Specify the DeletionPolicy attribute in the definition of both resources to be imported. Each resource to be imported must have this attribute for the import to succeed, and specifying Retain is safe.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Turn on termination protection for the stack so that the stack is not deleted even if the import fails partway, and the existing resources are automatically attached to the stack while termination protection is on.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Set a stack policy on both resources that denies all update actions until the import is finished, and release the policy after the import is complete to allow template changes.

explanation: The correct answers are specifying DeletionPolicy on the resources to be imported, and specifying the resource identifiers in an import change set and running it. A resource import succeeds only when each resource to be imported has a DeletionPolicy attribute, maps the existing resources to the logical IDs in the template by using the identifier properties and actual values, and incorporates the existing resources into the stack as they are, without creating or deleting any resources. A stack policy is a means of protecting against updates and is not a condition required for import. Copying data and deleting the originals violates the requirement to import without deletion or re-creation. Termination protection only prevents stack deletion and has no function for attaching existing resources. The condition that there is no time or budget to copy tens of TB of data eliminates the copy-and-replace approach.

prompt: A financial services team stores more than 1,200 container images in an Amazon ECR private registry. Currently only basic scanning on push is enabled, so a CVE disclosed after an image is pushed is not discovered until the next build. Vulnerabilities in Java and Python libraries must also be detected, and an automatic notification must go to the security team's SNS topic when a new critical vulnerability appears. The security team wants to see the vulnerability status of the entire registry in one place during the monthly audit. The number of images to scan keeps growing, and many of them are stored for months without being newly pushed or run. Build pipelines differ by team, so modifications must be minimized. The images are spread across 40 repositories in the Seoul Region, and Java (Maven) and Python (pip) services are mixed. The security team wants to be notified the same day when new CRITICAL and HIGH vulnerabilities appear, and the build pipelines differ by team so they are hard to modify. The security team exports vulnerability results as a PDF report at the monthly audit, so it is important that the results are collected in one place. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Add an open-source image scanner to the AWS CodeBuild stage of all build pipelines to check for vulnerabilities at build time, fail the build if there are critical findings, and notify through Amazon SNS.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Set a lifecycle policy on each repository to delete images older than 30 days so that old vulnerable images do not remain in the registry, and notify of delete events through Amazon SNS.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Change the registry scanning configuration to enhanced scanning (Amazon Inspector integration) with continuous scanning and set the rescan duration based on the push date to Lifetime, and deliver high-severity Inspector finding events to the SNS topic with an EventBridge rule.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Keep basic scanning, have an EventBridge scheduled rule run a Lambda function every day that calls StartImageScan on all images, and receive scan completion events through EventBridge to forward them to Amazon SNS, where the Lambda function builds the list of images to scan by querying the repositories each time.

explanation: The correct answer is to turn on continuous scanning with enhanced scanning and set the rescan duration based on the push date to Lifetime. Enhanced scanning integrates with Amazon Inspector to check both operating system and programming language package vulnerabilities, updates the findings when a new CVE is disclosed, and emits EventBridge events. The default monitoring period is 7 days for newly enabled registries, so images that are stored for a long time without being touched would fall out of the rescan scope, and the Lifetime setting is therefore required. Basic scanning scans only operating system vulnerabilities, so it does not meet the Java and Python library requirement. A build-stage scanner misses CVEs disclosed after the push and also requires large pipeline changes. Deleting old images is image lifecycle management, not a means of detecting vulnerabilities. The condition that many images are stored for a long time without being touched makes it necessary to set the rescan duration to Lifetime.

prompt: The security team of a fintech organization wants to restrict scheduling of deletion of customer managed KMS keys (ScheduleKeyDeletion) so that only the security administration role can perform it, and to be notified within minutes when a key deletion is attempted. Administrators of the 20 member accounts can change IAM policies in their own accounts, so this restriction must not be bypassable by them. A key scheduled for deletion must be cancellable by the security team during the waiting period, but unauthorized scheduling attempts must be blocked in the first place. This requirement arose after an incident in which a former employee scheduled key deletion and it was only discovered later. The organization already uses SCPs, and an organization CloudTrail trail is turned on in all accounts. The waiting period after scheduling deletion is already standardized at 30 days. The security administration role is a single SecurityAdmin role in the security account, and the application roles in member accounts only use the keys. This measure must be maintained without manual work by the security team even as the number of accounts grows. The deletion-scheduling notification should be delivered to both the security team's chat channel and email. Which combination is MOST appropriate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Deploy a deny statement for kms:ScheduleKeyDeletion to the IAM policies of each account with StackSets, and replace notifications with a monthly CloudTrail log review.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Set the key policy to deny deletion scheduling, and receive notifications by viewing AWS Config rule evaluation results after the key goes into a pending deletion state.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Apply an SCP that denies deletion scheduling to principals other than the security administration role, and receive CloudTrail events through Amazon EventBridge and send notifications through Amazon SNS.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Set the deletion waiting period for all keys to the shortest, 7 days, and have the responsible person cancel it in the console within 7 days if deletion is scheduled.

explanation: The combination of an SCP deny and an EventBridge notification is the correct answer. An SCP is a ceiling that member account administrators cannot change, so it prevents deletion scheduling by anything other than the security administration role, and receiving the ScheduleKeyDeletion call recorded in CloudTrail through EventBridge delivers a notification within minutes. Account IAM policies can be modified by account administrators, and a monthly log review has too much notification delay. A key policy change can be reverted by the account's key administrators, and Config evaluation is after-the-fact detection with delay. The waiting period is a value specified at scheduling time and is not a preventive measure, and leaving the cancellation to a person is a structure that is easy to miss. The condition that member account administrators can change IAM policies makes an SCP the only preventive measure that cannot be bypassed.

prompt: The SRE team at a food delivery app company wants to handle assignment of owners, status tracking, and linking of related resources and runbooks in one place when an Amazon CloudWatch alarm goes into ALARM. There are dozens of alarms per day, there is no dedicated development staff, and the company must use only AWS services without adopting an external ticketing system. Each incident must retain its action history and owner, and when an alarm occurs, ticket creation must happen automatically without human handling. Currently the team manages alarms with email notifications and a shared spreadsheet, and owners have often been missed. The team already uses AWS Systems Manager for instance management. The OpsItem must record the owner, priority, and related resources, and the post-incident retrospective reconstructs the timeline from them. The team operates in a single account in the Seoul Region. At night one person is on call, so when an alarm fires, the responder must be able to open the OpsItem on a mobile device as well. The OpsItem title must show the alarm name and severity so that the responder can set priorities. Which solution has the LEAST operational overhead, given that development and maintenance must be minimal?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Add an OpsCenter OpsItem creation action to the alarm actions, link the related resources and runbooks to the OpsItem, and have the owner update the status.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Send an Amazon SNS email as the alarm action and set a procedure in which the owner manually records the incident status and owner in a shared spreadsheet.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Invoke a Lambda function from the alarm to create your own ticket table in Amazon DynamoDB, and develop a web screen yourself for assigning owners and updating status.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Place an alarm status widget on a CloudWatch dashboard and operate by having the shift worker watch the screen and assign the owner verbally.

explanation: An OpsCenter OpsItem is the correct answer. When a Systems Manager action is added to the alarm actions, an OpsItem is created automatically on ALARM, and the OpsItem manages the owner, status, related resources, and runbook links in one place, so no additional development is needed. Email and a spreadsheet make status tracking manual and prone to omissions and duplicates. A DynamoDB ticket system and a web screen must be developed and maintained by yourself, which has the highest operational overhead. Dashboard watching and verbal assignment leave no record and require staff to keep watching the screen. The conditions that a ticket is created automatically when an alarm occurs and that no external SaaS is used eliminate the email and spreadsheet approach.

prompt: A securities company wants to protect its Amazon RDS and Amazon EBS backups against ransomware and insider threats. The requirements are that backups must not be deleted even if the production account is compromised, and that no one, including the root user, can delete a backup or change the retention policy before the retention period (minimum 35 days). All accounts belong to the same AWS Organizations organization, and the scenario in which administrator permissions of the production account are stolen must be assumed. A copy of each recovery point must also exist in a separate account that production account administrators cannot access. Backups are already performed once a day with AWS Backup, and the company does not want to change the backup tool. The backup targets are 30 RDS instances and 200 EBS volumes, and the backup plan is deployed through an Organizations backup policy. A dedicated backup account has already been created in the organization, and recovery drills are performed every six months from this account's recovery points. The additional cost of creating copies of recovery points has already been approved in the security budget. A restore test of the recovery points is performed once every six months to verify that they are usable. Which configuration is MOST appropriate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Set up cross-account copy to a vault in a separate dedicated backup account, apply a vault lock in governance mode to that vault, and grant the permission to change the retention period only to the security team's IAM role.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Set up cross-account copy to a vault in a separate dedicated backup account, and apply a vault lock in compliance mode (grace time of 3 days or more, minimum retention of 35 days) to that vault.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Export the backups to an Amazon S3 bucket, store them in a bucket in a separate account, and turn on S3 Object Lock in governance mode and MFA Delete so that objects cannot be deleted for 35 days.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Apply a vault lock in compliance mode to the same vault in the production account, deny backup deletion for all principals with the vault access policy, and specify a retention period of 35 days or more.

explanation: The correct answer is a configuration that copies across accounts to a dedicated backup account and applies a compliance mode vault lock. In compliance mode, once the grace time ends, the lock and the vault can no longer be changed or deleted, so neither the root user nor AWS can delete a backup before the retention period, and because a copy exists in a separate account it survives a compromise of the production account. The grace time must be at least 3 days. Governance mode allows a user with sufficient permissions to remove the lock, which violates the requirement that no one can delete. Keeping backups only in the same account does not protect against a compromise of the production account. S3 Object Lock in governance mode can also be bypassed by a privileged user. The scenario in which the production account administrator permissions are stolen and the requirement that even the root user cannot delete eliminate governance mode and same-account storage.

prompt: A fintech company publishes its internal package @corp/billing-utils to an npm repository in AWS CodeArtifact, and this repository has an upstream repository with an external connection to the public npmjs registry. The security team is concerned about a dependency substitution attack, in which an attacker uploads a higher version with the same name to the public registry so that builds pull a malicious version. The 80 developers must continue to publish internal packages directly, and must be able to download other public packages as usual. Packages are published and installed many times a day, so slowing down the development flow or adding a separate approval step is unacceptable. The build environments are a mix of developer PCs, per-team CI servers, and AWS CodeBuild, so it is hard to control client settings one by one. Internal package names all use the @corp scope, and the repository administrator is the security team. The build environments are a mix of developer PCs, per-team CI servers, and CodeBuild, so it is hard to control client settings one by one. An external audit last quarter pointed out the risk of dependency substitution attacks. The security team wants to be able to prove with logs that builds did not pull a malicious version even if a dependency substitution attack occurs. Which prevention measure is MOST appropriate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Remove the external connection from the repository and change the development procedure so that developers download all public packages themselves and publish them manually to the internal repository.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Set the package origin controls of that internal package to allow publish and block upstream, so that even if a version with the same name is uploaded to the public registry, it cannot enter the repository.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Specify in the .npmrc on developer PCs and build servers that packages in the @corp scope are downloaded only from the internal repository, and distribute this setting in the team development guide document.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Change the upstream repository connection order so that the public repository has the lowest priority, and set a rule that internal package versions are always published with the latest tag.

explanation: The correct answer is to set the package origin controls to allow publish and block upstream. With this setting, direct publishing continues to work and versions with the same name do not flow in from the public registry or upstream repositories, so the dependency substitution attack is blocked, and other packages are unaffected. Removing the external connection violates the requirement to download public packages as usual. Specifying the scope in .npmrc depends on client settings, cannot block inflow at the registry level, and leaves risk in any environment where the setting is missing. The connection order and tags are not a means of preventing an external version with the same name from flowing into the repository. The condition that client settings cannot be controlled eliminates the .npmrc approach.

prompt: In the 60 accounts of a logistics group's organization, if S3 Block Public Access on a bucket is turned off, it must be turned back on automatically without human intervention. Even when a new account is added to the organization, the same detection and remediation must apply without separate work, and the security team manages the rules in only one place, the delegated administrator account. Remediation is done by turning on the Block Public Access settings, and the IAM role used to run remediation is not created by hand in each account but is deployed with the same name to all accounts with StackSets so that it is provided consistently. Currently the owner of each account receives an email alert and handles it manually, which takes hours. The security team has 3 people and cannot maintain per-account automation code. The remediation history must be viewable at once from the delegated administrator account, and rule changes must be made by editing one template and redeploying it. After remediation, a follow-up notice that tells the bucket's owning team the result is needed, but this notice is outside the scope of this question. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

choices.label: A
choices.text: From the delegated administrator account, define in an organization conformance pack template an S3 Block Public Access AWS Config rule and an AWS Systems Manager Automation automatic remediation action, specify the StackSets-deployed role as the AutomationAssumeRole, and deploy it to the organization.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Create AWS Config rules directly in each account, have the owner who receives the noncompliance notification by email turn the Block Public Access setting back on in the console, receive per-account reports of the results, and create the same rules manually in new accounts as well.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Deploy separately, with AWS CloudFormation in each account, an Amazon EventBridge rule that detects PutBucketPublicAccessBlock calls from AWS CloudTrail events and a Lambda function, and manage the deployment status of each account separately.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Receive AWS Security Hub organization integration findings as a report once a day, have the security team correct the bucket settings of all accounts at once with a batch script, include new accounts starting from the next report, and keep the remediation history in the script logs.

explanation: An organization conformance pack is the correct answer. A conformance pack bundles Config rules and remediation actions into a single template and deploys it to the entire organization, and remediation is performed by an SSM Automation document whose execution role is deployed to all accounts with the same name through StackSets and specified as the AutomationAssumeRole, which satisfies single-place management in the delegated administrator and automatic application to new accounts. Creating rules in each account and having owners remediate manually misses both the automatic remediation requirement and the automatic application to new accounts requirement. The CloudTrail call event approach sees only the call that turns protection off, and does not solve buckets that are already noncompliant or the per-account deployment management. Remediating with a script after a daily report requires human intervention and has a large delay. The condition that rules must be managed with a single template eliminates deploying event rules per account.

prompt: A reservation platform automatically rotates the application account password of Amazon RDS for MySQL with AWS Secrets Manager every 30 days. The application uses a connection pool and rereads the secret every 5 minutes. High availability requirements are strict, so the possibility that a request that read the secret during rotation is denied authentication must be reduced as much as possible. Secrets Manager rotation continues to be used, and the cloned user may have the same permissions as the original user. Failed rotations must be retried automatically, and the company does not want to create a procedure to redeploy the application or restart the connection pool because of rotation. The operations team has 4 people and there is no separate maintenance window. The database is Multi-AZ, and the application servers run 20 tasks concurrently on Amazon ECS. The rotation Lambda function runs in the same VPC as the database, and a Secrets Manager VPC endpoint already exists. A requirement that the previous credentials the application was using must not be invalidated immediately during rotation has already been confirmed in the security review. The rotation schedule is set for the early morning of the first week of each month, but retries on failure must be automatic. Which solution is MOST appropriate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Use the single user strategy and add a deployment procedure that restarts the connection pool so that the application reads the new secret right after rotation finishes.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Read the secret value only once at application startup and keep it in an environment variable, and set a procedure in which the responsible person performs rotation manually at deployment time.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Use the alternating users rotation strategy and keep a separate superuser secret for cloning the user.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Limit the rotation schedule to a nighttime maintenance window only, and block application traffic during the maintenance time so that authentication denials do not occur.

explanation: The alternating users strategy is the correct answer. This strategy updates two users in turn, so an application that read the secret during rotation still gets valid credentials, and after rotation both the previous user and the cloned user remain valid, so the chance of authentication denial is lowest; a separate superuser secret for cloning is required. The single user strategy has a risk of denial in the short interval after the password changes and before the secret is updated. Fixing the value in an environment variable and rotating manually abandons the automatic rotation requirement. A nighttime maintenance window and traffic blocking conflict with the high availability requirement. The condition that the company does not want to create a procedure to restart the connection pool eliminates the single user strategy.

prompt: The AWS Security Hub delegated administrator account of an e-commerce organization aggregates findings from 70 accounts. A large volume of findings for a specific LOW-severity S3 control accumulates in 12 accounts in the development OU and clutters the security team's queue. The same findings in production accounts must still be shown as they are, and the control check itself must continue in all accounts. The history of suppressed findings must remain for audit purposes, and the security team wants to change the suppression criteria in one place. The security team has 2 people and cannot maintain additional code or per-account configuration. Security Hub is aggregated in the Seoul Region and the AWS Foundational Security Best Practices standard is turned on. The suppression target is a control related to access logging on development buckets, the 12 accounts in the development OU are identified by account ID, and there are 40 accounts in the production OU. The security team wants to be able to easily audit the scope of impact of the suppression rule in the console. The suppression rule must not be managed as code, and the security team must be able to check and modify it in the console. Which solution meets these requirements while minimizing the number of rules to manage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Disable the control across the entire organization to stop generating findings, so that the same findings are no longer shown in the production accounts either.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Deploy an Amazon EventBridge rule and a Lambda function in each development account to suppress findings with BatchUpdateFindings whenever a new finding is generated.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Have the security team filter and select the development account findings in the console once a week and manually suppress them by setting the workflow status.

choices.label: D
choices.text: In the delegated administrator account, create an automation rule that changes findings matching the development account IDs, LOW severity, and the control ID to SUPPRESSED.

explanation: An automation rule in the delegated administrator account is the correct answer. For new and updated findings, an automation rule changes the workflow status to SUPPRESSED when conditions such as account ID, severity, and control ID match, and when created once in the administrator account it applies to all member accounts (the rule operates only in the Region where it was created). Disabling the control stops the check itself and loses both the production account findings and the check requirement. Per-account EventBridge and Lambda would require deploying and maintaining code in 12 places. Weekly manual suppression leaves the queue cluttered in the meantime and repeats manual work. The conditions that production account findings must still be shown and the checks must continue eliminate disabling the control.

prompt: A payment service team wants to verify, in a pre-production environment that matches production, that the payment success rate is maintained even if one of the three Availability Zones in the Seoul Region disappears. The experiment injects a failure that stops the Amazon EC2 instances in one Availability Zone, and if the payment success rate Amazon CloudWatch alarm drops below 99%, the experiment must stop automatically before a human intervenes. The experiment procedure must be kept as a repeatable definition, and the results must be compared each time by using the same procedure. The experiment runs only in a production-like environment, and the permission to run the experiment is limited to an IAM role with the minimum scope. The team wants to repeat the same experiment every quarter and does not want to maintain its own fault injection code. All target EC2 instances have the tags Env=staging and Tier=payment and run in an Auto Scaling group. The payment success rate is measured continuously during the experiment, and the experiment results are compared at each quarterly retrospective. The experiment is performed during business hours after advance notice, and the target is limited to the payment service in the staging environment. Which solution BEST meets these requirements?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Create a Lambda function that calls the EC2 stop API and a Lambda function that polls the alarm state and restarts instances, tie them together with AWS Step Functions, and keep the experiment procedure as a state machine definition.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Have an engineer stop the instances in that Availability Zone manually in the console while watching the alarm dashboard, and manually restart the stopped instances if anything abnormal is seen.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Remove that Availability Zone from the Auto Scaling group's Availability Zone list to terminate the instances, and manually run a CloudFormation stack update that adds the Availability Zone back if the alarm fires.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Define in an AWS FIS experiment template a stop action that selects the EC2 instances in the target Availability Zone by tag, specify the payment success rate alarm as a stop condition, and run the experiment.

explanation: The correct answer is to define a stop action and a stop condition in an AWS FIS experiment template. FIS lets you define an experiment as a template that can be run repeatedly, and when the CloudWatch alarm specified as a stop condition crosses its threshold, the experiment stops automatically, which satisfies the requirement that it stops before a human intervenes. A stopped experiment cannot be resumed, but that is suitable for a safeguard. Manually stopping in the console violates the requirements for automatic stopping and a repeatable definition. Building it with Lambda and Step Functions requires implementing the safety mechanism and the restart logic yourself. Removing the Availability Zone from the group is a configuration change, not fault injection, and recovery is also manual. The condition that the company does not maintain its own fault injection code eliminates the Step Functions approach.

prompt: A shopping app company deploys a service running on AWS Fargate with rolling updates (the Amazon ECS deployment controller) several times a day. Yesterday it deployed a new task definition, and because of a defect in which the container exits right after starting, the new tasks repeatedly failed and restarted, and the deployment remained in progress for a long time. Without adopting AWS CodeDeploy blue/green and while keeping the existing rolling update method, the company wants a deployment like this to automatically return to the last successfully completed deployment when it is judged to have failed. While the new tasks are failing, the existing tasks must continue to handle traffic, and no human judgment should be needed for the return. The development team does not want to change the structure of the deployment pipeline. The service uses ALB target group health checks, 10 tasks are distributed across 3 Availability Zones, and the deployment configuration is already a minimum healthy percent of 100% and a maximum percent of 200%. It must be possible to confirm from the service events which healthy version it returned to on rollback. The return to the previous healthy deployment must proceed without a separate approval process, and service notifications are maintained after rollback. Which solution is MOST appropriate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Turn on the deployment circuit breaker with the rollback option so that a deployment is judged FAILED on repeated failures and returned to the last COMPLETED deployment.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Change the deployment configuration to a minimum healthy percent of 100% and a maximum percent of 200% so that existing tasks are taken down only when all new tasks are healthy.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Implement and connect your own rollback code in which a Lambda function specifies the previous task definition with UpdateService when a CloudWatch alarm fires.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Switch the service to the CodeDeploy blue/green deployment controller and use AppSpec hooks and alarm-based rollback to revert a failed deployment.

explanation: The rollback option of the deployment circuit breaker is the correct answer. The circuit breaker marks a deployment FAILED when new tasks cannot reach RUNNING or repeatedly fail health checks and reach the threshold, and if the rollback option is on, it returns to the last COMPLETED deployment, so it can be used while keeping rolling updates. Adjusting the minimum and maximum percentages helps keep healthy tasks but has no failure judgment or automatic return, so the new tasks keep retrying. A self-built rollback Lambda function has implementation and maintenance burden. Switching to blue/green violates the constraint of not adopting it. The background that the percentage settings are already applied means adjusting the percentages has no new effect.

prompt: A retail group must centrally manage operating system patching of 400 Amazon EC2 instances across 5 accounts and 3 Regions. A scan to collect compliance information must run every day, installation must run only at 2 AM on Sunday, and security updates must be auto-approved only after 7 days have passed since release. Reboots caused by patching are allowed only early on Sunday morning. For security audits, the patch compliance status per instance must be viewable in the Systems Manager compliance view of each account and Region. The infrastructure team has 3 people and wants to avoid creating maintenance windows and associations separately for each account and Region. The instances are a mix of Amazon Linux 2023 and Windows Server 2022, and all are registered as Systems Manager managed instances. The patch targets are instances tagged Env=prod, and changes to the patch policy must be made by the central team in one place. After the Sunday 2 AM installation window has passed, the instances that need a reboot must be identifiable in an inspection report. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Create State Manager associations in each account and Region to run AWS-RunPatchBaseline as a Scan operation daily and as an Install operation at 2 AM on Sunday, and create a 7-day auto-approval baseline in each account and set it as the default.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Create a maintenance window in each account and Region and register an AWS-RunPatchBaseline task, group instances with the Patch Group tag, and create a 7-day auto-approval baseline by hand in each account and associate it with each group.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Install an Ansible agent on the 400 instances to update packages by cron early on Sunday morning, and aggregate the compliance status of all accounts with a script that uploads per-instance results to Amazon S3.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Create a patch policy with Systems Manager Quick Setup integrated with AWS Organizations, define the scan and install schedules separately, specify a patch baseline that auto-approves security updates after 7 days, and apply it to the target OUs and Regions.

explanation: A Quick Setup patch policy is the correct answer. A patch policy integrates with Organizations and is applied to managed nodes across multiple accounts and Regions with a single configuration, can specify different schedules for scanning and installing, lets you choose the patch baseline per operating system so the 7-day auto-approval baseline can be used, and the compliance information produced by scans is reported for each account and Region pair, which meets the audit requirement. The maintenance window and Patch Group approach still requires repeating the setup for every account and Region combination. State Manager associations also have to be created for each account and Region, which increases repetitive work. Ansible does not use the Systems Manager patch baseline and compliance reporting features and has to be built yourself, so it has the highest operational overhead. The condition that settings must not be repeated for each account and Region puts the maintenance window and State Manager association approaches at a disadvantage.

prompt: A securities company must deliver Amazon EC2, Amazon RDS, and Application Load Balancer metrics in three Regions to a third-party APM and an Amazon S3 data lake for long-term analysis in near real time. Currently a Lambda function polls the metrics with GetMetricData every 5 minutes, but the API call cost is high and delivery latency reaches several minutes. Only metrics in the EC2, RDS, and ALB namespaces need to be included, and a setup that operates a separate collection server in each Region is not allowed. The APM can receive data at an HTTP endpoint, and the data lake loads data into partitioned paths in S3. The observability team has 3 people and cannot easily maintain metric collection code. The metrics center on EC2 CPU, RDS connection count, and ALB request count, and the delivery targets are the three Regions of Seoul, Tokyo, and N. Virginia. The APM can accept the OpenTelemetry format, and the data lake may store data in the original format. Metric latency of about 1 minute in near real time is sufficient, and no metrics may be lost during delivery. The company will not add a separate processing step for metric format conversion and wants to handle it with the delivery services alone. Which solution reduces delivery latency and operational overhead the MOST?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Reduce the interval of the EventBridge scheduled rule to 1 minute so that the same Lambda function calls GetMetricData for EC2, RDS, and ALB metrics more often and sends the results to S3 and the APM separately, deploying the function in each Region.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Additionally install the APM vendor's agent on each server and database to send metrics directly, configure the agent to upload to S3 separately, and supplement managed service metrics with the agent.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Create two CloudWatch Metric Streams in each Region with a filter that includes only the EC2, RDS, and ALB namespaces, and send one to Amazon Data Firehose for S3 and the other to Firehose for the APM's HTTP endpoint.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Create an Observability Access Manager sink in a central account, allow the APM service to create a link to read CloudWatch metrics, and set up a separate export for S3.

explanation: Metric Streams connected to Firehose is the correct answer. A stream exports metrics in near real time, a namespace filter can select only the EC2, RDS, and ALB metrics, and Firehose delivery streams for S3 and for the APM HTTP endpoint each deliver to their destinations, so the polling code and GetMetricData call cost go away. Reducing the polling interval to 1 minute actually increases the API call cost and leaves the code maintenance burden unchanged. Adding the APM agent to servers requires host changes, and the agent cannot collect managed service metrics such as ALB and RDS. An Observability Access Manager link is for sharing observability data between AWS accounts, so an external APM cannot create a link. The condition that no collection servers may be placed in each Region eliminates the agent approach.

prompt: The operations team at a service company must apply a configuration change runbook to 200 Amazon EC2 instances tagged Env=prod in one account in the Seoul Region. The change must proceed in stages of 10% of the total at a time and must stop automatically if failed instances exceed 5%. In addition, before it is applied to the first target, one of two operations owners must approve, and the approval request must be announced through Amazon SNS. Connecting to the instances with SSH or placing a self-managed script server is not allowed. The work history must be retained for audit per execution step, and the operations team performs the change itself using a runbook created as code. The instances are already registered as SSM managed instances and the Automation execution role is also ready. The change runbook consists of steps that replace a configuration file and restart the service, and the approval request is delivered to an SNS topic subscribed to by the two operations owners. The change history must let auditors confirm, per execution step, who approved and on which instances a failure occurred. Instances that fail during the work are reprocessed separately later, and this requirement is limited to staged progress and stopping. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Place an aws:approve step (two approvers, minimum approvals of 1, SNS notification) as the first step of a Systems Manager Automation runbook, run the change runbook against the tag-based targets in the next step with aws:executeAutomation, and specify a maximum concurrency of 10% and a maximum error of 5%.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Have an AWS Step Functions state machine process the instance list in batches of 20 in a Map state, implement yourself an approval step using a callback token and a failure counter that stops the execution when it exceeds 5%, and keep the per-step history in the state machine execution record.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Run the script on the tag-based targets with Run Command with a maximum concurrency of 10% and a maximum error of 5%, and document a procedure to obtain verbal approval by email from one of the two operations owners before the run.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Distribute SSH keys to the instances and have a shell script on a bastion host run repeatedly in 10% batches, with the script exiting when the number of failures exceeds 5% and approval obtained by chat.

explanation: The correct answer is to place an aws:approve step in a parent runbook, run the child change runbook against the tag-based targets with aws:executeAutomation, and specify the maximum concurrency and maximum errors. aws:approve pauses execution until the required number of the designated approvers approve and sends a notification to the SNS topic; approval is obtained only once in the parent runbook, and the child execution's maximum concurrency of 10% and maximum error of 5% handle staged progress and automatic stopping. If the approval step were put in the execution against the targets itself, the child automation for each target would repeat the approval step. Run Command relies on verbal approval, so approval is not enforced by the system. Step Functions requires implementing and maintaining the approval and failure counter yourself, which has a large operational overhead. SSH and a script server directly violate the constraint that they cannot be used. The condition that SSH and a self-managed script server cannot be used eliminates the bastion approach.

prompt: The trading system of a securities firm runs active-passive in two Regions, Seoul and Tokyo. By regulation, an operator must explicitly press a failover button when a Region fails, and the setup must prevent an incident in which the traffic of both Regions is turned off at once during a failure. In addition, the failover operation must not depend on modifying Route 53 records, which is a control plane API that can be affected during a failure. Failover drills are held every quarter, and the drills must be validated by using the same procedures and tools as during a real failure. Both Regions have identical configurations prepared behind an Application Load Balancer, and DNS is already operated in a Route 53 hosted zone. Cross-Region data replication is already configured, so this question covers only traffic failover. Normal traffic goes 100% to Seoul, and the operations team wants to judge the failover state by a value explicitly set by the operator, separate from ALB health checks. The failover procedure document used in the quarterly drills must be kept identical to what is used in a real failure. The results of the quarterly drills are evaluated by failover time and whether the safety rules work. Which configuration is MOST appropriate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Create routing controls per Region and routing control health checks in an Application Recovery Controller cluster, associate them with Route 53 failover records, and add a safety rule requiring that at least one remain on.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Keep Route 53 weighted records at Seoul 100 and Tokyo 0, and use a runbook in which the operator changes the weights to Seoul 0 and Tokyo 100 with the Route 53 API during a failure. The change is made with the Route 53 API, and after the change the operator directly checks the healthy state of both Regions.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Have the operator change the traffic dial of the AWS Global Accelerator endpoint groups to Seoul 0 and Tokyo 100 during a failure, and directly check the healthy state of both Regions before and after the change.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Associate the health check of each Region's ALB with Route 53 failover records so that when the Seoul health check fails, traffic switches to Tokyo automatically without human intervention and returns when recovered.

explanation: ARC routing controls and safety rules are the correct answer. A routing control is a simple on/off switch that shifts traffic from one Regional replica to another, works with Route 53 health checks to drive the failover records, and is operated through the data plane of a cluster made up of endpoints in five Regions, so it does not depend on the control plane. A safety rule that enforces at least one remaining on prevents the incident in which both are turned off at once. Changing weights is a control plane operation, which violates the dependency constraint. Automatic failover based on health checks violates the regulation that a person must perform the failover directly. A traffic dial is also a control plane operation and has no safety rules. The condition that the solution must not depend on the control plane API eliminates the weight change approach.

prompt: A SaaS company manages a monorepo on GitHub (12 services) and operates a separate AWS CodePipeline pipeline for each service. Currently the pipelines run no matter where in the repository a push occurs, so the orders service pipeline runs unnecessarily dozens of times a day because of unrelated service changes, and cost is increasing. The company wants the pipeline to run only when files under services/orders/ change on the main branch, without operating a new Lambda function or Amazon EventBridge rule, and with minimal changes. A new service is added every quarter, so the same approach must be repeatable as services increase. The source is already integrated through a GitHub connection (AWS CodeConnections). The repository has 12 directories under services/ and a common libs/ directory, and the orders service pipeline does not need to react to changes in libs/. The pipeline consists of AWS CodeBuild and AWS CodeDeploy stages. The finance team pointed out that although the cost of a single pipeline execution is small, it adds up to a meaningful monthly cost when it accumulates dozens of times a day. Which solution BEST meets these requirements?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Migrate to separate repositories per service, create a repository dedicated to the orders service, and have the pipeline run when a push occurs to that repository.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Change the pipeline type to V2 and add a push trigger to the source action that uses the GitHub connection, specifying filters of main for the branch and services/orders/** for the file paths.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Turn off change detection on the source action of the V1 type pipeline, add a CodeBuild action after the source stage, and have it exit with an error code if the list of changed files does not include the orders service path.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Create an Amazon API Gateway and a Lambda function that receive GitHub webhooks, inspect the changed file paths, and call StartPipelineExecution only when the paths match.

explanation: The correct answer is to change the pipeline to type V2 and apply push trigger filters to the connection-based source action. Branch and file path filters are supported only in the V2 type, and when specified, the pipeline starts only for pushes that match the conditions, so no additional infrastructure is needed and the change is small. Exiting early with CodeBuild on V1 still incurs the pipeline execution and source stage cost and leaves a failure status. Adding API Gateway and Lambda conflicts with the constraint of not operating anything new. Migrating to separate repositories is a larger change than the requirement calls for and violates the minimal-change requirement. The condition of not operating new infrastructure eliminates the API Gateway and Lambda approach.

prompt: The web application of an online education company runs in an Auto Scaling group (8 instances) behind an Application Load Balancer. Some instances fall into a deadlock and do not respond to requests, while the EC2 status checks pass and the ALB target group health check marks those instances as unhealthy and removes them from traffic. However, the instances remain and capacity decreases. The application takes about 4 minutes to initialize after boot. Traffic is normally 800 requests per second, and adding instances increases cost, so the problematic instances must be replaced quickly without needlessly increasing capacity. The replacement must be performed by Auto Scaling without human intervention, and the company does not want to build its own monitoring code. The ALB target group checks the /health path every 10 seconds, and the unhealthy threshold count is 2. The Auto Scaling group currently uses EC2 health checks with a grace period of 0 seconds, and a new instance always takes less than 4 minutes to come up healthy. Replacement instances are always created from the same AMI and launch template, and the ALB sends requests only to healthy instances even during replacement. Which setting is MOST appropriate to replace unhealthy instances automatically while keeping a new instance that is still booting from being terminated early?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Keep the Auto Scaling group health check type as EC2 and set the grace period to 0 so that an instance is replaced immediately when a problem occurs in the EC2 status checks.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Turn on the Elastic Load Balancing health check type in the Auto Scaling group and set the health check grace period to 300 seconds, which is longer than the initialization time.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Reduce the health check interval and unhealthy threshold count of the ALB target group so that instances are judged unhealthy sooner, and keep the Auto Scaling group health check settings at their defaults.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Turn on detailed instance monitoring and configure an EventBridge rule so that when a CPU utilization alarm fires, a Lambda function terminates that instance, replacing unresponsive instances yourself.

explanation: The correct answer is to turn on the ELB health check in the Auto Scaling group and set the grace period longer than the initialization time. By default, Auto Scaling ignores ELB health check results and uses only EC2 status checks, so the ELB health check must be turned on for it to replace instances that the load balancer reports as unhealthy. The grace period must be longer than the initialization time so that an instance that is still booting is not caught by the check and replaced repeatedly. Adjusting only the ALB health check makes removal from traffic faster but no replacement occurs. A CPU alarm and Lambda termination cannot reliably indicate a deadlock through a metric and would have to be implemented yourself. Using only EC2 status checks cannot detect an application deadlock. The condition that the initialization time of a new instance is about 4 minutes calls for a grace period longer than the initialization time.

prompt: A bank has a pipeline named MyFirstPipeline that has a manual approval action in the stage right before the production deployment. By regulation, only the release manager group can approve, and developers may view the pipeline status but must not be able to approve their own changes. The approval request must also be delivered by email. The approval history must let auditors confirm who approved and when, and even if the number of pipelines grows beyond 20 as services increase, approval permission settings must be easy to maintain. The developer group already has permission to view pipelines. The approval action is a single ManualApproval in the prod-deploy stage, and all pipeline names follow the prod- convention. Release managers sign in with roles imported from IAM Identity Center, and audit evidence is checked with the PutApprovalResult event in AWS CloudTrail. There are 5 release managers, and approval permission must not automatically follow when a new developer joins. The people who receive the approval request email may include development leads who do not have approval permission. Which configuration meets these requirements MOST appropriately while following the principle of least privilege?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Attach the AWSCodePipeline_FullAccess managed policy to the release manager group, and separately attach to the developer group an explicit deny policy that denies only PutApprovalResult from that policy to block approval only. An explicit deny takes precedence over an allow, so the developer group's approval denial remains in effect.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Specify an SNS topic on the manual approval action and connect an email subscription, allow the codepipeline:PutApprovalResult permission to the release manager group only, with the approval stage and action ARNs of the pipelines as the resource, and give the developer role view permissions only.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Grant the developer group AWSCodePipelineApproverAccess, and add a Lambda verification step after the approval action that fails the pipeline if the author of the change approved it, blocking self-approval.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Do not use the manual approval action; have a CodeBuild stage check for the existence of an approval file, and restrict with a bucket policy so that only release managers can upload the file to that S3 location.

explanation: The correct answer is a manual approval action connected to SNS notifications, with the PutApprovalResult permission scoped to the approval action ARN and granted only to release managers. The approval permission can be limited to an individual action with a resource ARN in the pipeline/stage/action format, which follows least privilege. Granting a full access policy and blocking with a deny is a configuration that grants needlessly broad permissions. Using an approval file does not use the pipeline's standard approval feature, notifications, and audit records and is a self-built control with a large operational overhead. Giving developers approval permission and blocking self-approval afterward with Lambda violates the regulation that developers must not have approval permission in the first place. The condition that permission settings must stay easy to maintain as pipelines grow fits well with scoping the resources by the naming convention.

prompt: An online bookstore has an active-passive configuration in which the Application Load Balancer in the Seoul Region is the primary endpoint and the ALB in the Tokyo Region is the standby endpoint. If the Seoul ALB has no healthy targets, DNS must automatically respond with the Tokyo ALB. The company wants to minimize creating and managing separate health check resources, and failover must occur without human intervention. The RTO is within 5 minutes, and depending on a procedure in which a person edits DNS records directly at night would delay the response. DNS is already operated in a Route 53 hosted zone, and both ALBs are in the same account. Both ALBs are internet-facing in their respective Regions, and the domain is in a Route 53 hosted zone. The Seoul ALB target is a single Amazon ECS service, Tokyo keeps only standby capacity normally, and it is acceptable for traffic to return to Seoul automatically when Seoul recovers. The Tokyo data is replicated asynchronously from Seoul, and this question covers only the DNS failover method. The time it takes to fail back after the Seoul ALB's healthy targets recover is not important. Which Route 53 configuration has the LEAST operational overhead?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Create two alias records (primary and secondary) with the failover routing policy that target the ALB in each Region, set Evaluate target health to Yes, and do not associate a separate health check.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Create latency-based alias records in the two Regions with Evaluate target health turned off, and prepare a runbook in which the operator deletes the Seoul record if Seoul fails.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Put both IP addresses of the Seoul ALB and the Tokyo ALB as values in a single simple routing record, and set the TTL as short as possible so that clients use whichever responds.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Configure an EventBridge rule and a function so that when a CloudWatch alarm that monitors the ALB's healthy host count goes to 0, a Lambda function modifies the Route 53 record to point to the Tokyo ALB.

explanation: The correct answer is a failover alias record with Evaluate target health turned on. An alias record that targets an AWS resource such as an ALB does not require creating a separate health check; if Evaluate target health is set to Yes, Route 53 follows the target's health and responds with the secondary record when the primary record is unhealthy. A simple routing record does not evaluate health, so an unhealthy IP is included in the response, and lowering only the TTL does not produce automatic failover. A latency record with Evaluate target health turned off cannot detect a failure and requires manual deletion. Modifying records with an alarm and Lambda must be implemented yourself, so the operational overhead is large. The condition of minimizing separate health check resources supports the configuration that uses the alias record's Evaluate target health.

prompt: The large-file upload API of a photo printing service runs in an Auto Scaling group behind an Application Load Balancer, and a single upload request takes up to 90 seconds. Every time a scale-in or an unhealthy instance replacement occurs, uploads in progress are cut off and 5xx errors occur. The deregistration delay of the target group is set to 30 seconds, which is shorter than the default. Scale-in happens several times a day, and interrupted uploads lead to customer complaints. The application code cannot be changed, and the maximum time for one request to finish does not exceed 90 seconds. The ALB forwards HTTP/1.1 requests to the target group, and the scale-in policy is target tracking based on CPU utilization. An upload is a single HTTP request that completes within one request and has no resume feature, and the maximum upload time of 90 seconds is a value agreed as a service level objective. The client does not automatically retry when an upload fails, so the interruption itself must be prevented. The instance that is terminated during scale-in may always have an upload request in progress. Which action is MOST appropriate to prevent upload interruption while meeting these requirements?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Increase the Auto Scaling group health check grace period to 120 seconds so that an instance selected for termination keeps serving longer until it finishes in-flight requests.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Set the target group deregistration delay to 120 seconds, which is longer than the longest request time of 90 seconds, so that Auto Scaling waits to terminate a terminating instance until it finishes in-flight requests.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Change the termination policy to NewestInstance so that the most recently launched instances are terminated first, keeping the older instances that handle uploads for a long time from being terminated.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Increase the target group health check interval to 90 seconds so that an instance with an upload in progress stays in a healthy state, and also increase the unhealthy threshold count so that fewer replacements occur.

explanation: The correct answer is to set the deregistration delay longer than the longest request time. With connection draining on, Auto Scaling waits until in-flight requests finish or the maximum wait time passes before terminating the instance, so increasing the delay to 120 seconds lets all 90-second requests finish, and the interruption goes away without any code change. The health check grace period is a setting that delays the start of checks for newly launched instances and is unrelated to waiting at termination. Adjusting the health check interval changes only how fast an instance is judged unhealthy and does not wait for in-flight requests at termination time. Changing the termination policy only changes which instance is terminated and does not solve the problem of requests being cut off on whichever instance is terminated during scale-in. The condition of a single request with no resume feature means a setting that waits for in-flight requests at termination time is needed.

prompt: A healthcare company rotates the password of an Amazon RDS database in a private subnet with an AWS Secrets Manager Lambda rotation function. The VPC has no internet gateway and no NAT gateway, and the database is not exposed externally. The rotation function code uses the AWS-provided template as is, and the database has no public IP. By security regulation, traffic to the database and to Secrets Manager must not traverse the internet, and adding a new NAT gateway has not been approved. The rotation period is 30 days. The rotation function's subnets span 2 Availability Zones, and the database security group currently allows only port 3306 from the application subnets. The function code uses the AWS-provided template without modification, and because approving code changes to the rotation function is difficult, the company does not want to add custom code other than the template. How the application connects with the new password after rotation is outside the scope of this question. Which TWO configurations that let the rotation function connect to the database and call Secrets Manager meet these requirements in the SAFEST way? (Select TWO.)

choices.label: A
choices.text: Leave the Lambda function outside the VPC and allow port 3306 from 0.0.0.0/0 in the inbound rules of the database security group so that the rotation function can connect.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Store the database password in plaintext in a Lambda environment variable and update the function configuration each time it is rotated, removing the Secrets Manager call.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Attach an internet gateway to the VPC and change the database subnet routing to public so that Lambda reaches the database and Secrets Manager over the internet.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Create a Secrets Manager interface endpoint in the VPC so that Lambda reaches the service without traversing the internet.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Connect the rotation Lambda function to the same VPC subnets as the database, and use security groups to allow only the connection between Lambda and the database.

explanation: The correct answers are connecting Lambda in the same VPC and a Secrets Manager interface endpoint. The rotation function must reach both the database and the Secrets Manager endpoint; placing it in the same VPC as the database and allowing the connection with security groups lets it connect without exposing the database, and in a VPC with no internet, an interface endpoint lets it reach the service privately. Attaching an internet gateway and making the database subnet public puts the database at risk. Keeping the password in a plaintext environment variable defeats the protection of Secrets Manager. Allowing 0.0.0.0/0 inbound leaves the database open to the whole world. The condition that adding a NAT gateway has not been approved eliminates the configurations that go over the internet and supports the endpoint approach.

prompt: The order API of a delivery platform deploys a Lambda function with an AWS SAM template. A new version must initially receive only 10% of invocations, and after watching the error alarm for 10 minutes, the rest must be shifted. Before the shift begins, a smoke test function must validate the new version, and if an alarm fires, the deployment must be rolled back to the previous version without human intervention. This function receives hundreds of invocations per second, and even a brief rise in error rate leads to lost orders, so the number of customers affected by the new version must be limited during the first 10 minutes. The team wants to meet this requirement only by modifying the existing SAM template, without adopting a new deployment tool. The function is invoked behind Amazon API Gateway, and CloudWatch alarms for the Errors and Throttles metrics already exist. The SAM template is deployed from a CI pipeline that has a service role that can use AWS CodeDeploy, and the smoke test function has already been written as a separate SAM resource. This function is deployed three times a week, and having a person watch the deployment progress every time is hard to sustain. What is the SIMPLEST solution?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Use the canary deployment setting of the API Gateway stage to send 10% of traffic to the new API deployment, have an operator promote the canary in the console after 10 minutes, and delete the canary deployment to roll back if there is a problem; in this method, the entire API deployment, not a Lambda alias or version, is the canary target.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Specify AutoPublishAlias on the function, set DeploymentPreference to Canary10Percent10Minutes, and specify the smoke test function in the PreTraffic hook of Hooks and the error alarm in Alarms.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Set DeploymentPreference to AllAtOnce, run the smoke test in a PostTraffic hook, and have the AWS CloudFormation stack rollback revert to the previous version if the test fails.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Deploy the new version as a separate function, split two API endpoints with Route 53 weighted records at 10 to 90, and configure a CloudWatch alarm action to invoke a Lambda function that reverts the weights.

explanation: The correct answer is to use DeploymentPreference in SAM. AutoPublishAlias creates an alias, Canary10Percent10Minutes shifts 10% first and moves the rest after 10 minutes, the PreTraffic hook validates before the shift, and CodeDeploy rolls back automatically when an alarm in Alarms fires. API Gateway canary works at the API deployment level, not at the Lambda version level, and promotion and rollback are manual operator tasks. AllAtOnce does not shift 10% first, so it does not meet the required staged shift, and PostTraffic validates after the shift is finished. Using a separate function and Route 53 weights can implement the requirement, but you would have to build and operate the records and the alarm-reaction logic yourself, so it is not the simplest. The conditions that no new tool is adopted and only the SAM template is modified, and the requirement for a shift at the Lambda alias level, support DeploymentPreference.

prompt: A travel platform team uses AWS CodeDeploy to deploy an application to 30 Amazon EC2 instances. The ApplicationStop script of the last successful revision has an error and always returns a nonzero exit code. The new revision includes a fix to this script, but deployments keep failing at the ApplicationStop stage. The problem must be solved by deploying this revision without re-creating the instances or the deployment group. Production traffic is flowing to the target instances, so manually connecting to each instance to fix the script is not allowed. A hotfix must be deployed today. The deployment group selects instances by EC2 tags, and automatic rollback is turned off. The new revision is already uploaded to Amazon S3, the fixed ApplicationStop script has been verified locally, and the hotfix must be deployed today. Some files left by the previous deployment do not conflict with the new revision, so the file overwrite problem is irrelevant to this requirement. Deployment logs are checked in the CodeDeploy console, and the agent version is the latest. Which action is MOST appropriate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Delete the deployment group, re-create it with the same name, and deploy the new revision so that the information about the previous revision is reset and the script does not run.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Reinstall the CodeDeploy agent on each instance to reset the agent state so that the new revision's AppSpec and scripts are also used at the ApplicationStop stage.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Increase the timeout of the ApplicationStop hook in the new revision's AppSpec to 3600 seconds so that the previous revision's script has enough time to handle the error and exit normally. Also analyze the logs and adjust the time value so that the previous revision's script exits normally within the time limit.

choices.label: D
choices.text: When creating the deployment, specify the option that ignores failures of the ApplicationStop lifecycle event (--ignore-application-stop-failures) and deploy the new revision that includes the fixed script.

explanation: The correct answer is to deploy with the option that ignores ApplicationStop failures. ApplicationStop runs the AppSpec and script of the last successful revision, not of the current revision, so even if the script is fixed in the new revision, the old script with the error runs in the first deployment and fails. If you deploy once while ignoring the failure, the fixed script is used from then on. Increasing the timeout does not fix the defect that the script always returns a nonzero code, and that script belongs to the previous revision, not the new revision's AppSpec. Re-creating the deployment group changes the cleanup information that was managed under the existing deployment group ID and can cause file conflict errors. Reinstalling the agent has nothing to do with which revision's script is used. The condition that the deployment must be done today without connecting to instances or re-creating the group supports the ignore-failure option.

prompt: At an online shopping mall, 40 Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group behind an Application Load Balancer serve a web application. The company uses CodeDeploy in-place deployments, and the deployment lifecycle takes about 3 minutes per instance. Even during deployment, at least 75% of all instances must always be in a healthy serving state, and the entire deployment must finish within 30 minutes. None of the predefined deployment configurations meets both conditions. Traffic is highest during the daytime and there is little spare capacity per instance, so if service capacity runs short during deployment, order failures increase. The team has no budget to add instances. The instances span three Availability Zones, and CodeDeploy is configured to deregister instances from the ALB target group before deployment and register them again after deployment. Most of the lifecycle time is the application shutdown time in BeforeInstall and is similar across instances. If an instance fails the health check between the start and end of deployment, that instance is treated as failed at that stage. Which solution has the LEAST operational overhead?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Use CodeDeployDefault.HalfAtATime but increase the instances to 60 so that service capacity remains sufficient even while half are being deployed at the same time.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Use CodeDeployDefault.OneAtATime and split the deployment group into 4, configuring parallel actions in the pipeline so that four deployments start at the same time.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Use CodeDeployDefault.AllAtOnce but remove all instances from the ALB before the deployment starts to show a maintenance page, and register them again when the deployment ends.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Create a custom deployment configuration that specifies a minimum healthy host value of 75%, apply it to the deployment group, and turn on the load balancer connection and automatic rollback on deployment failure in the deployment group.

explanation: The correct answer is a custom deployment configuration with a minimum healthy hosts value of 75%.
