Deploying 10 instances at a time, which is 25% of 40, takes about 3 minutes for each of 4 batches and finishes in about 12 minutes, with at least 75% always in service. HalfAtATime deploys half at the same time, so the healthy percentage drops to 50% and violates the 75% condition; adding instances does not change the percentage criterion and only increases cost. OneAtATime deploys 40 instances sequentially, taking about 120 minutes and violating the 30-minute limit, and splitting groups to parallelize makes the configuration complicated. AllAtOnce deploys to all instances at the same time and directly violates the 75% service requirement. The condition that there is no budget to add instances eliminates solving it by adding capacity.

prompt: The audit team of a manufacturing group needs to identify, within one day, which currently running EC2 instances across 70 accounts and 4 Regions of the organization were created from AMIs that are not on the approved list. It wants to query from a single account and avoid logging in to each account or running scripts that repeatedly call service APIs. The AWS Config recorder is recording EC2 instances in all accounts. The results are submitted as audit evidence, and the audit team has no permission to log in to individual accounts and must query all account data from only one account. This check is repeated every quarter, so it would be good if the query can be reused. The list of approved AMI IDs has about 120 entries and is managed in one account as a Systems Manager parameter. The query results must include the account ID, Region, instance ID, and AMI ID, and there are about 6,000 instances. The audit team downloads the query results as CSV and submits them as evidence, and query cost is not a concern. The target instances do not include terminated ones, and only the current configuration state is needed. Which solution is MOST appropriate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Run a script that iterates over each account and Region calling DescribeInstances, and merge the results to create a report that compares them with the approved list.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Create an organization AWS Config aggregator in the delegated administrator account that includes all accounts and Regions, and use an advanced query to find instances whose imageId is not on the approved list.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Query the RunInstances event history of the organization trail with Amazon Athena in 90-day units to estimate the currently running instances and AMIs.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Check the number of failed EC2-related controls in the AWS Security Hub organization summary dashboard to find instances with unapproved AMIs.

explanation: A Config aggregator and an advanced query are the correct answer. An aggregator gathers configuration data from multiple accounts and Regions in one place, and an advanced query reads the current resource state with SQL-like syntax, so you can find instances by an imageId condition without logging in to accounts or calling service-specific APIs. A script that iterates over accounts and Regions calling DescribeInstances is the approach the question asks to avoid. RunInstances events are past launch records, so the current running state would have to be estimated, and it is hard to distinguish terminated instances. The number of failed Security Hub controls does not provide information for matching against the approved AMI list. The condition that the same query can be reused every quarter also supports a saveable advanced query.

prompt: At an e-commerce company, applications in multiple accounts each write JSON logs to their own Amazon CloudWatch Logs log groups. The security team wants to gather the logs of all accounts in an Amazon S3 bucket in a separate log archive account within minutes, but the current script that runs CreateExportTask daily in each account has a large delay and does not meet the requirement. The logs come from 40 accounts at hundreds of GB per day, there must be no loss in transit, and the company does not want to grant S3 write permissions to any account other than the archive account. The application and log agent configuration cannot be changed. The logs come from 40 accounts in the Seoul Region, and the archive account is also in the Seoul Region. The security team queries S3 with Amazon Athena, so it wants files to be loaded under time-based prefixes, and the ingestion delay must be within 5 minutes. One JSON line is one event, and some log groups have different retention periods, so the archive account wants everything to accumulate in the same format. The archive account's bucket is open for write-only access and the source accounts have no read permission. Which configuration meets the near-real-time delivery requirement with the LEAST operational overhead?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Place a Lambda function in each account that polls the log groups with GetLogEvents every minute and saves directly to the archive account's S3 bucket with PutObject.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Change the export task schedule from daily to hourly and have each account call CreateExportTask with an EventBridge scheduled rule.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Create a Logs destination in front of Amazon Data Firehose in the archive account and deliver to S3 through subscription filters on each account's log groups.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Change the agent configuration so that the CloudWatch agent on each instance assumes an IAM role in the archive account and writes directly to log groups in the archive account.

explanation: The combination of a Logs destination in the archive account and subscription filters is the correct answer. A subscription filter sends log events to Firehose in near real time and Firehose loads them into S3, so it satisfies both the latency requirement and the requirement of no application changes. A polling Lambda function requires maintaining code and checkpoints in every account, so the operational overhead is large, and the latency is bound by the polling interval. An export task is an asynchronous batch job, so even a shorter schedule does not meet the near-real-time requirement. Having the agent write to log groups in another account requires changing the settings on all hosts and building the S3 loading path separately. The condition that the agent and the application cannot be changed eliminates changing the agent configuration.

prompt: In the Workloads OU of a telecom company's AWS Organizations organization there are 60 accounts, and accounts will continue to be added. The security team wants to deploy, with AWS CloudFormation, an IAM role for delivering audit logs and AWS Config rules to the Seoul and Tokyo Regions of all accounts. When a new account joins the OU, deployment must happen automatically, and if deployments fail in 3 or more accounts in a Region, the operation must stop immediately. Management account credentials are not used for day-to-day operations, and the deployed stack must be the same template in all accounts. If manual work arises per account, it becomes hard to prove consistency in an audit. The StackSet template consists of one IAM role and two Config rules and is deployed to the Seoul and Tokyo Regions at the same time. When the template changes, the security team wants to update it in one place and have it reflected in all accounts, and failed accounts can be retried separately later. The audit team wants to view the deployment status of each account on a single screen. The target Regions are only Seoul and Tokyo, and no additional Regions are planned. Which solution has the LEAST operational overhead?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Place CloudFormation deployment actions for each account in parallel in AWS CodePipeline, and when a new account is created, update the CDK code to add an action to the pipeline and redeploy.

choices.label: B
choices.text: In a delegated administrator account, create a StackSet with service-managed permissions that targets the OU, turn on automatic deployment, and set the failure tolerance to 2.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Use a StackSet with self-managed permissions, manually create a StackSet execution role in each account, have a Lambda function add a StackSet instance on every new account creation event, and set the failure tolerance to 2.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Create a service-managed StackSet in the management account that targets the OU but turn off automatic deployment, have the responsible person add newly created accounts to the target list every week, and set the failure tolerance to 2.

explanation: The correct answer is a service-managed StackSet in a delegated administrator account with automatic deployment turned on and the failure tolerance set to 2. With service-managed permissions, StackSets creates the necessary IAM roles and, through automatic deployment, creates stacks in new accounts that join the OU, and using a delegated administrator means management account credentials do not need to be used day to day. Failure tolerance is calculated per Region, so it continues when up to 2 accounts fail and stops at the third failure. Self-managed permissions require creating roles and handling events yourself, and turning off automatic deployment means new accounts are not deployed automatically and the management account must be used. Per-account pipeline actions require code changes every time accounts are added. The conditions of automatic deployment to new accounts and not using management account credentials support service-managed permissions and a delegated administrator.

prompt: A CI pipeline pushes images to an Amazon ECR private repository in the tooling account of a financial group, and dozens of new images are pushed every day. Amazon ECS tasks in 15 workload accounts in the same AWS Organizations organization must pull these images, and the repository settings must not need to be edited each time a new workload account is added to the organization. Storing separate copies of the images in each account is not acceptable because of cost. The security team requires that access be strictly limited so that accounts outside the organization cannot pull the images. The platform team has 3 people, so onboarding an account must not involve manual work. The ECS tasks in the workload accounts run on AWS Fargate, and the task execution roles are created with the same naming convention in each account. The repository and all workload accounts are in the Seoul Region, and image pull speed is not a concern. Some other repositories in the tooling account are exposed to external partners under a separate policy, and this must not be mixed with that policy. Each workload team is responsible for approving changes to the task execution role on the pulling side. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Manage a repository policy that lists the workload account IDs as individual Principals with an AWS CloudFormation StackSet, and update the target list and policy statements and redeploy every time a new account is created. Also configure a CI job in which the pipeline reads the target list and redeploys the StackSet when a new account is created.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Create an ECR read-only IAM user in the tooling account, store the access keys in AWS Secrets Manager, and have the tasks in each account log in to the tooling account registry with these keys to pull images.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Create an ECR repository in each workload account and replicate images to each account with replication rules from the tooling account repository so that tasks pull from the repository in their own account.

choices.label: D
choices.text: In the tooling account repository policy, allow ecr:BatchGetImage and ecr:GetDownloadUrlForLayer with the aws:PrincipalOrgID condition specifying the whole organization, and grant the authorization token and pull permissions to the task execution role in each account.

explanation: The correct answer is to allow pulls for the whole organization by using the aws:PrincipalOrgID condition in the repository policy. When a new account joins the organization, it gets access without a policy change, the images are stored only in the tooling account so there is no replication cost, and each task execution role must have the permission to obtain an authorization token through its IAM policy. Listing account IDs requires a policy update for every new account, which violates the requirement. Per-account replication multiplies image storage cost by the number of accounts, which is a prohibited condition. Sharing long-term access keys carries a heavy key management and rotation burden and goes against security best practices. The condition that repository settings must not be edited when a new account is added supports the organization ID condition.

prompt: The platform team at a game publisher wants to let 30 development teams create Amazon RDS and security group stacks themselves. Developers must not have IAM permissions for RDS, EC2 security groups, or AWS CloudFormation directly, and they must be able to choose the DB instance class only from three approved options. The product must be usable from multiple development accounts in AWS Organizations. New development teams join every quarter, so this setup must be maintained without manual work by the platform team as the number of teams grows. Developers prefer to select a product from a list in the console and enter only values. Development teams cannot decide encryption and backup retention period themselves when creating RDS and use values fixed in the template. For a new version of the product, the platform team edits and publishes the template and the development teams choose to update, and the development accounts are under the development OU. The platform team must be able to change only the template constraint and publish it when the approved instance classes change. All DBs created by the development teams are placed in private subnets in the Seoul Region. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Give developers only the permission to create CloudFormation stacks and have the stack create resources with a service role, but developers write the templates themselves and the instance class is checked in code review.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Create a new account for each development team with AWS Control Tower Account Factory, include the RDS and security group stacks in the account creation template, and have developers modify them directly in the account.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Register a CloudFormation product in an AWS Service Catalog portfolio, specify an IAM role for provisioning as a launch constraint, limit the instance class to the three options with a template constraint, and share the portfolio with the organization.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Give developer roles full permissions for RDS, security groups, and CloudFormation in each development account, and limit the allowed scope by using an SCP that denies creating DBs with unapproved instance classes.

explanation: The correct answer is a configuration that uses Service Catalog launch constraints and template constraints. A launch constraint specifies the IAM role that Service Catalog assumes when provisioning a product, so end users can launch the product without holding permissions for the underlying services. A template constraint limits parameter values such as the instance class to an allow list, and sharing the portfolio makes it available in multiple accounts. Granting developers permissions directly violates the requirement that they must not hold them. Having developers write their own templates means the system cannot enforce the allowed classes. Account Factory is an account provisioning tool, and its purpose is not to provide a product list and restrict values. The condition that developers must not be given permissions directly supports the configuration that uses a launch constraint.

prompt: A ticket booking company collects Amazon API Gateway access logs (JSON) in Amazon CloudWatch Logs. The company wants to continuously check whether 5xx responses are concentrated on a small number of client IPs and to receive an alarm when the contribution of the top IPs grows. There are tens of thousands of unique IPs, and log ingestion reaches hundreds of GB per day. The company wants to view the top contributors by log field as a real-time time series without people running queries repeatedly. During an incident the responder has no time to build per-IP aggregations by hand, so the alarm must react automatically to changes in the top contributors. The log format is already unified as JSON, so no change is needed on the ingestion side. The API Gateway access logs are in JSON format and include the clientIp, status, and routeKey fields. The alarm only needs to fire when the 5xx count of the single top contributor exceeds a certain value, and the service runs in a single Seoul Region. It is enough for the alarm to fire when the top contributor's 5xx count exceeds a certain value as a 5-minute average. The rule must remain in place after the alarm clears so that it is ready for the next anomaly. Which solution has the LEAST operational overhead?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Run a Logs Insights query manually in the console every 5 minutes to aggregate 5xx counts per IP, and have the responsible person check the result to judge whether the threshold was exceeded.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Create a metric filter that uses the IP value as a dimension to produce a 5xx metric, and create one alarm for each individual metric that is generated for every unique IP.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Create a Contributor Insights rule on the log group with the IP field as the key and status 5xx as the filter, and set an alarm on the rule metric.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Trace all 5xx requests with an AWS X-Ray sampling rule, and have the responsible person compare error rates per client IP in the service map.

explanation: A Contributor Insights rule is the correct answer. It uses a log field as the contributor key to produce the top N contributors and the number of unique contributors as a real-time time series, and an alarm can also be set on the rule metric, so no one needs to run queries repeatedly. Running Logs Insights periodically is not real time and requires continuous human involvement. A metric filter that uses the IP as a dimension requires a separate metric and alarm for every unique IP, and with tens of thousands of them cost and management burden explode. X-Ray is a request-level tracing tool and is not suited to aggregating the top contribution of client IPs as a time series. The condition that there are tens of thousands of unique IPs eliminates the metric filter approach that uses the IP as a dimension.

prompt: The integration test stage of an AWS CodeBuild project at an insurance company needs the staging database password. The security team requires that the password must not remain in plaintext in the project environment variables or in the source repository, and that builds must always use the latest value without changing the build configuration even when the password is rotated automatically every 90 days. This build runs dozens of times a day, and multiple developers can view the project settings. Builds must not fail because the password was rotated, and no one should have to fix the settings. The buildspec is in an AWS CodeCommit repository, and the project runs in CodeBuild in the Seoul Region. The staging DB password is stored encrypted in AWS Secrets Manager with a customer managed KMS key, and rotation is performed by a Lambda function integrated with Amazon RDS. All developers can view the project settings, so the password value must not be exposed on the settings screen. The security team will check the password rotation history during audits, and the rotation history is viewed in Secrets Manager. Which actions are needed to meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead? (Select TWO.)

choices.label: A
choices.text: Store the password as a SecureString in AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store, read it with the parameter-store entry in the buildspec, and create a schedule for the responsible person to update the value every 90 days.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Store the password as a Secrets Manager secret, enable automatic rotation, and map it to an environment variable with the secrets-manager entry under env in the buildspec.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Grant the secretsmanager:GetSecretValue permission on that secret to the CodeBuild service role, and if a customer managed key is used, also grant decrypt permission on that key.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Put the password in the project environment variables as the PLAINTEXT type, and restrict CodeBuild console view permissions to the security team role only so that no one else can see the value.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Commit a file in which the password is encrypted with AWS KMS to the source repository, decrypt it during the build, and re-encrypt and commit the file every time it is rotated.

explanation: The correct answers are to store the password in Secrets Manager with automatic rotation enabled and map it in the buildspec, and to grant the build service role permission to read the value. The secrets-manager mapping in the buildspec retrieves the current version (AWSCURRENT) at build time by default, so no settings change is needed even after rotation, and retrieval fails if the service role lacks permission. A Parameter Store SecureString stores the value securely but has no automatic rotation feature, so a person has to update it, which does not meet the automatic rotation requirement. A plaintext environment variable can be exposed in plaintext in the console and CLI, so it is a prohibited approach. Committing an encrypted file leaves a secret in the source repository and requires manual work on every rotation. The automatic rotation requirement eliminates the Parameter Store approach, and the ban on plaintext exposure eliminates the environment variable approach.

prompt: A stack update for a logistics company's production stack failed and a rollback started, but someone had already deleted in the console the RDS parameter group that needed to be restored during the rollback, so the rollback also failed and the stack went into the UPDATE_ROLLBACK_FAILED state. In this state the stack cannot be updated. The parameter group that caused the problem cannot be recovered, but the stack must be recovered safely without deleting the stack or the remaining resources. While recovering, the other resources of the production stack, the Auto Scaling group and the Application Load Balancer, are still serving traffic, so they cannot be deleted or re-created. The incident happened in the morning and must be recovered today. The stack was in the middle of an update that replaces the parameter group in the template with a new name, and what was deleted is the parameter group with the old name. The console deletion cannot be undone, and the team plans to retry the update on the same day after recovery. The database and storage resources of the production stack are healthy and must not be touched during recovery. After recovery, the team plans to check the differences between the template and the actual resources with drift detection. Which solution is MOST appropriate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Delete the stack and create it again from the same template to provision all resources anew, and restore the data from the snapshot created at deletion to recover the service.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Create a change set that contains only a change adding the parameter group and run it on the stack in the UPDATE_ROLLBACK_FAILED state so that the missing resource is restored and the rollback then continues.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Run continue update rollback while specifying that the parameter group resource that failed to roll back be skipped, return the stack to UPDATE_ROLLBACK_COMPLETE, make the template and the actual resources consistent, and then update again.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Run the stack update again with the same template so that CloudFormation automatically re-creates the missing parameter group and the rollback is completed.

explanation: The correct answer is to run continue update rollback while skipping the failed resource. A stack in UPDATE_ROLLBACK_FAILED cannot be updated, but the rollback can be continued and returned to UPDATE_ROLLBACK_COMPLETE, and if the cause cannot be fixed, the resource that failed to roll back can be skipped to complete it. The skipped resource no longer matches the template, so it must be made consistent before the next update. Deleting and re-creating the stack creates all the remaining resources anew, which is an excessive recovery scope. In this state, stack updates and change set execution are not possible, so updating again or running a change set does not work. The condition that the Auto Scaling group and the ALB cannot be deleted eliminates deleting and re-creating the stack.

prompt: Under financial regulation, a securities group must retain management event audit logs for all accounts for 7 years and must be able to prove that the logs have not been tampered with or deleted. This is a newly built environment, and member account administrators must not be able to turn off or modify the trail. The logs must be producible immediately when a regulator requests them, and delete permission on the log store must not be granted to anyone during normal times. Audits are performed every year by an external auditor, and log retention is done in a separate archive account to reduce cost. The organization is AWS Organizations with all features enabled and has 80 accounts. Logs are stored in a dedicated Amazon S3 bucket in the archive account in the Seoul Region, and the regulator requires evidence showing that the logs have not been tampered with to be submitted together with the logs. The organization is AWS Organizations with all features enabled and has 80 accounts. After logs are delivered, access to the archive bucket must be allowed only for the audit role. Log storage cost is within the approved budget, and deletion for cost reduction is not considered. Which solution meets these requirements in the SAFEST way?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Create an individual trail in each account and have each account administrator retain logs in the account's own bucket, with a lifecycle rule that deletes them after 7 years.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Create an organization trail with log file integrity validation turned on in the management account, deliver it to S3 in the archive account, and apply S3 Object Lock in compliance mode for 7 years.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Create an organization trail and store it in an SSE-S3 bucket with only S3 versioning turned on to protect against deletion and overwriting, without using integrity validation.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Send the trail events of all accounts to Amazon CloudWatch Logs, set the log group retention to 7 years, and use this as the means of tamper prevention and integrity proof.

explanation: An organization trail with integrity validation turned on and Object Lock in compliance mode is the correct answer. An organization trail cannot be deleted or have its settings changed in member accounts, log file integrity validation proves tampering and deletion with hashes and signed digest files, and compliance mode Object Lock prevents anyone from deleting objects during the retention period. A per-account trail can be turned off by the account administrator, who can also erase the logs. Versioning alone allows someone with delete permissions to delete versions and does not prove tampering. Log group retention is not a tamper-proof means such as signed digests. The requirement to prove tampering needs log file integrity validation, and the condition that delete permission is not granted to anyone even during normal times supports compliance mode.

prompt: A fintech company's container images are pushed to Amazon ECR by an AWS CodeBuild pipeline. The audit requirements are that, in the production repository, no tag can be overwritten with a different image once it has been pushed, and that during an incident it must be possible to roll back to exactly the image that was deployed previously. The current pipeline pushes both a git commit hash tag and a latest tag with every build, and the Amazon ECS task definition references latest. In the past, an image with the same tag was overwritten and the cause of an incident could not be reproduced, so the auditor requires evidence that tags and image contents always correspond one-to-one. The company does not want to change the pipeline structure significantly. The repository is in a single Seoul Region, and an average of 200 production images are pushed per month. Deployment updates the ECS task definition through AWS CodePipeline, and rollback works by updating the service again to point to the image of the previous deployment. The development repository is excluded from this requirement. The pipeline's image tag convention uses both the build number and the commit hash, and this convention itself will not be changed. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST amount of change?

choices.label: A

choices.label: B
choices.text: Set the repository to immutable but specify only the latest tag as an exclusion filter so that latest can still be overwritten, and keep the ECS task definition referencing latest as it does now.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Turn on tag immutability for the repository, change the pipeline to push only the commit hash tag, and update the ECS task definition in the deployment stage to reference the commit hash tag.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Attach an IAM policy that denies ecr:PutImage to developer roles so that people cannot push directly, and allow only the pipeline role to push.

explanation: The correct answer is to turn on tag immutability and use only the commit hash tag. In an immutable repository, pushing with an existing tag returns ImageTagAlreadyExistsException, so continuing to push latest would make the pipeline fail, while using only unique tags means no tag is overwritten and the exact image of the previous deployment can be referenced for rollback. A configuration that exempts only latest violates the requirement that no tag can be overwritten. An IAM policy that blocks only developer pushes cannot prevent the pipeline from pushing again with the same tag. Lifecycle policies and replication are after-the-fact retention means and cannot prevent tag overwriting itself. The auditor's requirement for evidence that tags and images correspond one-to-one eliminates the approach that exempts latest.

prompt: Amazon GuardDuty at an e-commerce company produced a backdoor communication finding for an EC2 instance running in an Auto Scaling group behind a load balancer. The automated response workflow must preserve forensic evidence while minimizing service impact, must not terminate the suspected infected instance, and must keep the group's service capacity. The collected evidence will be used for follow-up investigation and regulatory reporting, so the disk state at the time of the incident must be preserved separately, independent of later changes. This process must run automatically, without paging anyone, even at night. The group is behind an Application Load Balancer and normally has little spare capacity. The instance belongs to an Auto Scaling group spread across 3 Availability Zones in the Seoul Region and has two EBS volumes (root and data). The automated response is run by AWS Step Functions after Amazon EventBridge receives the GuardDuty finding, and analysis is performed in a separate forensics account. The execution history of the response workflow is used as evidence in the incident report, so the result of each step must be retained. Which TWO actions should the workflow perform? (Select TWO.)

choices.label: A
choices.text: Terminate the instance immediately and let Auto Scaling replace it with a new instance, minimizing the time the suspected infected instance remains in service.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Reboot the instance to remove the malicious process residing in memory, and then leave it in the group as is to continue serving.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Create snapshots of the EBS volumes attached to the instance and preserve them as evidence for analysis.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Detach the instance from the Auto Scaling group and deregister it from the load balancer, and let a replacement instance launch without reducing capacity.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Immediately reset the passwords of all IAM users in the entire organization to block possible credential leakage all at once.

explanation: The correct answers are preserving EBS snapshots and detaching the instance from the Auto Scaling group. A snapshot leaves the disk state at that point in time as separate evidence without stopping or terminating the instance, and detaching the instance from the group deregisters it from the load balancer so traffic stops, and if you choose not to decrease capacity, a replacement instance launches and service capacity is maintained. Immediate termination loses evidence and violates the requirement not to terminate. A reboot erases memory evidence, and the malicious code on the same disk remains, so the infection continues. Resetting passwords of all users in the entire organization is an excessive measure unrelated to this instance compromise and greatly affects services and users. The requirements for automatic execution without paging anyone and for not terminating the instance eliminate immediate termination.

prompt: The development team at a game company wants to use CDK Pipelines to create a pipeline in the shared services account (111111111111) that deploys stacks to the Seoul Region of the staging account (222222222222) and the production account (333333333333). (Select TWO.)

choices.label: D

CDK Pipelines requires bootstrapping both the environment where the pipeline is created and the environments where stacks are deployed, and the bootstrap of a target environment must specify the pipeline account ID with --trust so that the pipeline in that account can assume the roles and deploy; the execution policies determine the deployment permissions of CloudFormation. Long-term access keys violate the constraint of not storing long-term credentials. Creating a pipeline in each target account breaks the structure of deploying from the shared account. A configuration that does not bootstrap the pipeline account omits the required environment preparation. The background that the target accounts do not yet have a place to upload assets makes bootstrapping the target environments necessary.

prompt: The payment API request count metric of a payment processor shows a pattern in which traffic concentrates during weekday daytime and drops sharply on weekends. A fixed-threshold alarm misses weekend drops if tuned to the weekday peak and produces repeated false positives on weekdays if tuned to weekends. The company wants to receive alarms only when the metric leaves its normal range for the time of day and day of the week, without people recalculating thresholds periodically. The alarm must detect both sharp drops and sharp increases, and the operations team does not want to adjust thresholds by hand. The metric has already been accumulating in Amazon CloudWatch for several weeks. The metric period is 1 minute, and there are special event days such as promotions about twice a year. Alarm evaluation at 5-minute intervals is sufficient, and the operations team wants to see the normal range band on a graph when the alarm fires. The metric has already been accumulating for several weeks. After the alarm fires, the on-call engineer checks the metric and the normal range together through the Amazon SNS notification. The alarm must work with one rule for both weekdays and weekends, and the company does not want separate alarms per day of the week. Which solution has the LEAST operational overhead?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Set a high fixed threshold based on the weekday peak value and disable the alarm actions on weekends with an EventBridge scheduler.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Have a Lambda function read last week's metrics with GetMetricData every week, calculate the mean and standard deviation, and update the threshold with PutMetricAlarm.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Enable CloudWatch anomaly detection on the metric and create an anomaly detection alarm that goes to ALARM when the value leaves the expected range band.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Change the request count metric statistic from the 1-minute average to p99, set the threshold once, and keep it fixed afterward.

explanation: An anomaly detection alarm is the correct answer. The anomaly detection model learns seasonality such as time of day and day of the week as well as trends, builds an expected range band, and raises an alarm only when the value leaves that band, so thresholds do not need to be recalculated. A fixed peak-based threshold plus disabling on a weekend schedule misses weekend drops and intra-day variation, and managing the schedule becomes a new burden. Recalculating weekly with Lambda is self-built code and has limits in reflecting changing patterns because it uses last week's statistics. Changing the statistic to p99 does not solve the time-of-day problem because the threshold stays fixed. The background that several weeks of data have already accumulated helps the anomaly detection model learn the day-of-week pattern.

prompt: GuardDuty is enabled in the 50 accounts of a telecom organization, and there is a security delegated administrator account. The company does not want to deploy rules to each member account or create cross-account event bus connections. The response must start within a few minutes of the finding, and the isolation action must be performed only with a least-privilege role in the target account. The number of accounts will keep growing, and the security team has 3 people. Findings occur in GuardDuty in the Seoul Region, and the SSM Agent is installed on the instances in member accounts. The isolation action is an Automation runbook that replaces the security group with an isolation security group, and an AutomationAssumeRole with the same name is deployed in every member account. Forensic analysis of the instance after isolation is performed in a separate security account and is not included in the scope of this question. The isolation targets are limited to findings that have high or higher severity and point to an EC2 instance. Which solution has the LEAST operational overhead?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Put a rule with a severity condition on the default event bus of the delegated administrator account, and isolate with Automation that assumes the role in the account indicated by accountId.

choices.label: B

choices.label: C

choices.label: D

In the delegated administrator account, its own EventBridge rule receives the finding events of member accounts as well, and the target account can be identified with detail.accountId, so there is no need to deploy anything per member account. Deploying rules and forwarding targets to each member with StackSets creates and maintains unneeded configuration in 50 places. Exporting to S3 and daily Athena queries introduce a delay of a day before isolation, which is unsuitable for automated response. A polling Lambda function per member requires operating code and schedules in every account and adds a 5-minute delay. The condition that rules must not be deployed to each member account eliminates the StackSets approach.

prompt: The payment API of a shopping app company runs as an Amazon ECS Fargate service. When the new version stabilizes, the old tasks must be cleaned up, and the service runs in a single Seoul Region. Payment processing must not be interrupted even during deployment windows, and the previous version must be able to receive traffic until the point of rollback. Which configuration meets all of these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Specify CodeDeployDefault.ECSCanary10Percent5Minutes in a CodeDeploy ECS blue/green deployment group, run the integration test with Lambda in the AfterAllowTestTraffic hook of the AppSpec, and connect the 5xx rate alarm as the deployment group's automatic rollback alarm.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Run an AWS Step Functions state machine from a CodePipeline invoke action to change the target group weights of the ALB listener rule in stages from 10% to 100%, and write it yourself so that the state machine restores the weights if an alarm fires.

choices.label: C

choices.label: D

explanation: The correct answer is a combination of CodeDeploy ECS blue/green deployment with ECSCanary10Percent5Minutes, the AfterAllowTestTraffic hook, and alarm-based automatic rollback. Test listener validation, the 10% 5-minute canary, and alarm rollback are all managed features, so no separate server or state machine is needed. Rolling updates with a circuit breaker only detect health check failures, so there is no test listener validation and no 10% first shift. ECSAllAtOnce moves all traffic at once, violating the requirement for a 10% first shift, and the rollback is a manual adjustment that requires human intervention. Changing weights with Step Functions can be implemented, but you must write and operate the state machine yourself, which conflicts with the constraint that no state machine can be operated. The condition of not operating a state machine and the requirement for CodeDeploy deployment records eliminate the Step Functions approach.

With a version wildcard for the parent image and a schedule conditioned on dependency updates, the pipeline runs automatically only when a new base AMI is released, an image that fails testing is not distributed, and the distribution settings deliver it to multiple Regions and accounts at once. Implementing it yourself with Lambda and EventBridge means maintaining both the orchestration and the error handling. The Packer approach has a person check for new base AMIs and start it, which violates the requirement for automation without human intervention. Having a pipeline in each account means operating 12 separate pipelines, which increases the burden and reduces test consistency. The condition that build and test cost is incurred only once eliminates the per-account pipeline approach.

prompt: A team at a media company performs CodeDeploy in-place deployments to Amazon EC2 instances. The new revision is set up so that the AfterInstall script creates the file /etc/app/feature.conf, but the ValidateService stage failed and an automatic rollback ran. After the rollback, the previous revision was deployed, but feature.conf remains on the instances and changes the behavior of the previous version. The operator wants to find the cause and prevent recurrence. The deployment procedure including the scripts is already used in the same way by several services, so changing to blue/green to replace instances is not part of this scope. There are 40 instances, and manually connecting to delete the file would not be a recurrence prevention measure. The previous revision in the rollback deployment already runs a service stop script in the BeforeInstall hook, so there is a place to put cleanup logic. feature.conf is not in the files section of the new revision's AppSpec and is created only by the script, and manually connecting to 40 instances to delete it is not a recurrence prevention measure. The operator wants to guarantee that the previous version operates without that setting even after a rollback. Which cause and action BEST fit this situation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A rollback reinstalls the last successful revision as a new deployment, and CodeDeploy deletes only the files installed by the previous deployment that are listed in the cleanup file, so files created by scripts remain. Add cleanup logic that deletes the file to the BeforeInstall hook script of the revision that is redeployed during rollback.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The content overwrite option for the deployment is set to Retain, so feature.conf was preserved. Changing the overwrite option to Overwrite when creating the deployment removes the file on rollback. This option must be specified each time a deployment is created and is applied the same way to later deployments.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The timeout of the ValidateService hook script is short, so the rollback deployment was interrupted midway. Increase the hook's timeout value so that the rollback deployment runs through all lifecycle events.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The CodeDeploy agent must be restarted after a rollback ends for the cleanup file to take effect. When the rollback completes, automatically run an operation that restarts the agent on all instances with Systems Manager.

explanation: The correct answer is to understand how rollback works and add cleanup logic to the script. CodeDeploy handles a rollback as a new deployment of the last successful revision, and before a new deployment it deletes only the files installed by the previous deployment that are listed in the cleanup file. Files that a script creates at runtime are not subject to cleanup and therefore remain, and since a rollback deployment runs the scripts of the revision being rolled back to, the deletion must be done directly in that revision's BeforeInstall hook. The overwrite option is how files that already existed at the target location are handled and does not delete files created by a script. A hook timeout would appear as a deployment failure and does not explain a file that remains after a successful rollback. There is no documented behavior in which restarting the agent applies the cleanup file. The fact that files created by scripts are not subject to CodeDeploy cleanup is the reason the cleanup logic must go in the script.

prompt: A healthcare data company's organization uses Amazon S3 buckets, IAM roles, AWS KMS keys, and Amazon SQS queues in three Regions. This analyzer uses the organization as the zone of trust, analyzes the policies of multiple resources such as S3, IAM roles, KMS keys, and SQS, and creates a finding for every access opened to an external principal; because analyzers are per Region, one must be created in each Region in use. Config rules require separate rules per service, and having people review the rest conflicts with the continuous detection requirement. Macie is a sensitive data detection service for S3 and does not look at IAM role and KMS key policies. GuardDuty centers on threat behavior detection and has only some findings related to S3 bucket policies; it does not continuously analyze whether the policies of IAM roles, KMS keys, and SQS queues are open to external parties, and there is no basis for treating an abnormal access finding as a policy change. prompt: A shopping platform deploys its Lambda-based order service with the AWS CodeDeploy Canary10Percent5Minutes configuration. Many deployments happen at night and no one can be on standby, and when the alarm threshold is exceeded the service must return to the previous version within a few minutes. The alarm evaluates the Errors metric as a 5-minute sum, the threshold has already been set based on operating experience, and there are a few deployments a day, mostly at night. It has been decided that, starting with this deployment, the procedure in which a person runs the rollback when the alarm fires will be eliminated. If a deployment is in progress when the alarm fires, the weights must immediately go back to the previous version. Which solution meets these requirements?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Write a runbook in which, five minutes after a deployment starts, the responsible person checks the alarm state and manually switches the weights to the previous version alias.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Receive the alarm state change event through Amazon EventBridge and implement code in which a Lambda function directly returns the weights to the previous version with UpdateAlias.

choices.label: C

choices.label: D
choices.text: Put validation logic in the PreTraffic hook Lambda function and judge that rollback after the shift is unnecessary because all errors are filtered out before traffic moves.

explanation: Alarm monitoring and automatic rollback configuration on the deployment group is the correct answer. When an alarm crosses its threshold or the deployment fails, CodeDeploy rolls back to the last healthy revision as a new deployment, so simply attaching the existing alarm rolls back without human intervention. A runbook for manual switching by the responsible person conflicts with the requirement to return before a person can look and reacts slowly. Returning the alias with EventBridge and Lambda can conflict with the weights that CodeDeploy controls and also requires self-built code. The PreTraffic hook validates only before the traffic shift, so it cannot detect an error rate increase that occurs after the shift. The conditions of not changing the existing alarm and minimizing pipeline changes support alarm monitoring on the deployment group.

prompt: The order processing Lambda function of a delivery app company calls PutMetricData synchronously on every request, which increases response time and occasionally causes throttling. Order throughput is several hundred requests per second, and the function's latency target is 200 ms or less. The team wants to use the metrics in alarms while keeping code changes small, and when a problem occurs wants to look up detailed attributes of the request (order ID, user ID) from the same log event. Unique values such as the order ID must not be made metric dimensions. It is sufficient for metrics to be reflected in alarm evaluation in 1-minute units, and the logs are already collected in CloudWatch Logs. The function is written in Node.js and already outputs structured JSON logs. The two metrics needed are OrdersProcessed and OrderLatencyMs, and the alarm is evaluated with a single service name dimension. The key goal of this change is to use the metrics in alarms without increasing the function's synchronous latency. The function's memory setting and timeout are left as they are, and only the logging approach is changed. Which solution is MOST appropriate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Batch the PutMetricData calls that were made for every request into a single call right before the function ends, and include the order ID in the dimensions for detailed tracking.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Create a metric filter that uses the order ID and user ID from every log line as dimensions so that a metric is created for each unique value, and set alarms only on the metrics that are needed.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Record the latency in AWS X-Ray annotations in the Lambda function and configure X-Ray group notifications so that an alarm fires based on the annotation value.

choices.label: D

explanation: EMF is the correct answer. The function only outputs a JSON log that contains the metric definitions, and CloudWatch extracts the metrics asynchronously, so the synchronous call latency and throttling of PutMetricData disappear, and unique values remain in the log as properties rather than dimensions and can be queried with Logs Insights. Batching still leaves an API call in the code, and including the order ID as a dimension creates a metric for every unique value and increases cost. A metric filter with unique-value dimensions explodes the number of metrics for the same reason. X-Ray annotations are for searching traces and are not for producing a base metric for alarms. The fact that the logs are already structured JSON means the code change to switch to EMF is small.

prompt: A fintech company updates an AWS CloudFormation stack that includes an Auto Scaling group and an Application Load Balancer every week. The company wants to monitor the alarm for 30 minutes after an update finishes and have the stack roll back to its previous state automatically, without human intervention, if the alarm fires. Updates are performed outside business hours and no one is on standby, so no human judgment may be involved from detecting the failure to recovery. The 5xx rate alarm has already been created in CloudWatch. The stack is in the Seoul Region, and the 5xx rate alarm to use as the rollback trigger has already been created in CloudWatch. Stack updates are run from a CI pipeline, and the usual update takes about 15 minutes. choices.label: B
choices.text: Specify both DeletionPolicy and UpdateReplacePolicy as Retain on the Auto Scaling group so that the existing group remains even if an update causes resource replacement.

choices.label: C

choices.label: D

After resource deployment finishes, CloudFormation watches the alarm for the specified monitoring time, and if the alarm goes to ALARM, it automatically rolls back the entire stack operation. The monitoring time can be set from 0 to 180 minutes, so it meets the 30-minute requirement. A stack policy is a means of blocking updates to specified resources and is unrelated to alarm-based rollback. Reviewing a change set and monitoring manually cannot cancel an update once it has already finished, and it involves a person. A deletion policy only preserves a replaced or deleted resource and does not trigger a rollback. The condition that rollback must happen without human judgment eliminates the manual monitoring approach.

prompt: A manufacturing company runs legacy applications on 60 VMware VMs (a mix of Windows and Linux) in its on-premises data center and wants to set up disaster recovery for them in AWS. The applications cannot be modified, the RPO is a few seconds, the RTO is within 1 hour, and normal-time AWS cost must be minimized. Recovery drills are held every quarter and must be repeatable without affecting production, and the impact on production performance of the source servers must be minimal. The recovery procedure is started by a person using predefined settings. The data center and AWS are already connected with AWS Direct Connect. Some of the 60 source servers run Windows Server 2016, which is an operating system supported by the replication agent. A staging subnet for replication can be created in AWS in advance, and DNS cutover after recovery is handled separately. The temporary instances used in recovery drills must be cleaned up after the drill so that costs do not continue to accrue. No person is involved in application initialization after the recovery servers boot. Which solution is MOST suitable to meet these requirements?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Back up the VMware VMs several times a day with AWS Backup and store them in a vault in an AWS Region, and when a failure occurs, restore servers from the backups to resume the service.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Run the same number of EC2 instances as on premises at all times in the AWS Region, continuously synchronize files and data with rsync, and shift only traffic when a failure occurs.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Install the AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery agent on the source servers to perform continuous block-level replication to a staging area subnet, and launch recovery instances only for drills and real failures.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Upload a nightly snapshot of each VM to Amazon S3, and document a procedure to create an AMI with VM Import/Export and launch new EC2 instances when a failure occurs. In this process, the boot verification and network configuration of the converted AMI are performed manually by the responsible person at the time of the failure.

explanation: AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery is the correct answer. It replicates the source servers' data continuously at the block level, so the RPO is on the order of a few seconds; it keeps replication in a staging area made of low-cost storage and minimal compute and launches recovery instances only for drills or failures, so normal-time cost is low, and it also supports drills that do not affect production. Nightly snapshots mean a day of data loss, which violates the RPO of a few seconds, and import and conversion also take a long time. Running the same number of instances at all times directly violates the cost minimization requirement, and the rsync setup must also be managed yourself. Backups several times a day lose the data between intervals and do not satisfy an RPO of a few seconds. The Direct Connect link is only a replication path and does not change the judgment that continuous replication is needed for an RPO of a few seconds.

prompt: The license server of a semiconductor design company runs on a single EC2 instance (using only an EBS root volume and no instance store volumes) that is tied to its instance ID and a fixed private IP. If a system status check fails because of an underlying hardware problem, the instance must be recovered automatically with the same instance ID and IP. OS errors inside the instance are handled separately. Recovery must be attempted automatically, and the operations team does not want to take manual action early in the morning. Reissuing the license takes several days, so creating a new instance is not an option. The instance is of a current-generation type that supports EC2 automatic recovery, and its EBS root volume is encrypted. After recovery, the attached network interface and the fixed IP must remain the same, and alarm notifications are also received through Amazon SNS. Because this server is a single instance, a high availability cluster configuration is not permitted under the license. When recovery occurs, the operations team only needs to receive the SNS notification, and no separate approval is required. Which solution meets these requirements with no additional server cost?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Configure the EC2 recover action on a StatusCheckFailed_System alarm (the default simplified automatic recovery for supported instances serves the same purpose).

choices.label: B
choices.text: Configure a CloudWatch alarm on the StatusCheckFailed_Instance metric that performs the EC2 reboot action so that the instance is restarted when a failure occurs.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Wrap the instance in an Auto Scaling group with a minimum of 1 and a maximum of 1 so that it is replaced with a new instance if it fails the health check.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Create AMIs regularly, and when a failure occurs have a Lambda function launch a new instance and attach the existing private IP to it.

explanation: The recover action connected to the system status check is the correct answer. Recovery moves the instance from the faulty host to another host and keeps the instance ID, the private and Elastic IP addresses, the metadata, and the attached EBS volumes as they are. An instance status check alarm is a metric that looks at OS-level problems and does not resolve a host hardware problem, and a reboot takes place on the same host. Auto Scaling replacement creates a new instance ID, which conflicts with the license requirement. Launching from an AMI also changes the instance ID and adds the burden of Lambda and AMI management. The condition that reissuing the license takes several days eliminates approaches that create a new instance.

prompt: The internal order system of a retail company consists of web and application servers in Seoul and Amazon Aurora MySQL. Management requires an RTO of 30 minutes and an RPO within a few seconds, and compute cost in the DR Region must be minimized during normal operation. A person may start the work of bringing up the service in the DR Region during a Regional failure, but the procedure must be automated, and the work of turning on the application servers in the DR Region during a failure can be automated with a template. DR drills are held twice a year. The budget is most sensitive to DR Region compute cost. The Aurora cluster has three db.r6g.2xlarge instances, and the application servers are 12 instances in an Auto Scaling group. The DR Region is Osaka, and IaC is AWS CloudFormation. No traffic is served in the DR Region during normal operation, and the storage cost in the DR Region is acceptable. DNS cutover during recovery is handled by a Route 53 change and is outside the scope of this question. Which DR strategy and configuration is the MOST cost-effective way to meet these requirements?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Pilot light: continuously replicate data to the DR Region with an Aurora global database, keep the application servers off with only the AMI and the IaC template prepared, and when a failure occurs, launch the servers from the template and scale them out.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Warm standby: always run a scaled-down full environment in the DR Region, replicate with an Aurora global database, and have part of the traffic handled even in normal times using Route 53 weighted distribution.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Backup and restore: copy daily DB snapshots and AMIs to the DR Region, and when a failure occurs, restore a cluster from the snapshot and create new servers from the IaC template to resume the service.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Multi-site active/active: operate full capacity in both Regions at the same time and have both Regions handle user requests by using the write forwarding feature of the Aurora global database.

explanation: Pilot light is the correct answer. Data is replicated continuously with an Aurora global database, which satisfies an RPO of a few seconds, and the application servers are only prepared with the AMI and IaC and kept off, so normal-time compute cost is lowest; during a failure, an automated procedure started by a person turns the servers on and scales them to aim for the 30-minute RTO. Backup and restore uses daily snapshots, which violates the RPO of a few seconds, and restore time is also long. Warm standby meets the requirements but runs a scaled-down full environment at all times, which is excessive compared with the requirement to minimize compute cost. Multi-site active/active maintains full capacity in both Regions and is the most expensive. The condition that DR compute cost is the most sensitive eliminates warm standby and multi-site.
